controls.title: Credential-less callers receive no identity at the API server
controls.objective: When anonymous authentication is on, a request carrying no credential is still admitted to the authorization stage as the user `system:anonymous` in the group `system:unauthenticated`, so the entire defence of the cluster rests on no RBAC object ever binding those subjects to anything useful. One over-broad ClusterRoleBinding then turns into unauthenticated cluster access from the internet. The API server should refuse the request at the authentication layer instead, and where a load balancer health probe forces anonymous access to remain on, it should be narrowed to the health endpoints alone.
controls.procedure: Pin the context on every call — `kubectl` acts on whatever `current-context` names, and that is global mutable state in the kubeconfig file — then record the endpoint so the evidence is attributable to the cluster in scope. Read the effective setting from the mirrored static pod: `kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.nodeName}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{"\n"}{end}'` and look for `--anonymous-auth`; the kube-apiserver default for that flag is true, so its absence is not safety. Where `--authentication-config` is set the flag may not be set alongside it and the anonymous stance lives in the AuthenticationConfiguration document instead, so resolve that file through the pod's `volumes` and `volumeMounts` and read its `anonymous.enabled` and `anonymous.conditions` fields. Then settle it behaviourally, which is also the only route where component configuration is unreadable: send a request carrying no credential at all to an endpoint that requires authentication, `curl -sk -i https://<apiserver_host>:6443/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/secrets`. HTTP 401 means the request was never given an identity. HTTP 403 whose body names `system:anonymous` means anonymous authentication succeeded and only RBAC refused — that is the failing state, not a passing one. Probe `/version` as the control case: the built-in `system:public-info-viewer` ClusterRoleBinding grants `system:unauthenticated` the health and version endpoints on every cluster, so 200 there alongside 401 on the secrets path is the expected shape of a hardened cluster and must not itself be read as a finding. Finally enumerate what the anonymous identity is actually granted with `kubectl --context <ctx> auth can-i --list --as=system:anonymous --as-group=system:unauthenticated`, capturing the exit status, and list every binding whose subjects name those principals — ClusterRoleBindings are cluster-scoped, RoleBindings are namespaced, so the RoleBinding sweep must carry `--all-namespaces` or it silently covers one namespace.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.nodeName}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{"\n"}{end}'

kubectl --context <ctx> get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(any(.subjects[]?; .name=="system:anonymous" or .name=="system:unauthenticated")) | "\(.metadata.name) -> \(.roleRef.kind)/\(.roleRef.name)"'

kubectl --context <ctx> get rolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(any(.subjects[]?; .name=="system:anonymous" or .name=="system:unauthenticated")) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name) -> \(.roleRef.kind)/\(.roleRef.name)"'
controls.evidence: The `--anonymous-auth` token, or its documented absence, taken verbatim from the container command array of each kube-apiserver pod and keyed by pod name and node; where `--authentication-config` is used instead, the `anonymous` block of the resolved AuthenticationConfiguration. The full status line and response body of the credential-less HTTPS request to the secrets path, retained because the distinction between 401 and a 403 naming `system:anonymous` is the verdict, together with the status code of the `/version` control probe. The rule list from `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:anonymous` with the command's exit status recorded alongside it, and the name plus `roleRef` of every ClusterRoleBinding and every namespaced RoleBinding whose subjects include `system:anonymous` or `system:unauthenticated`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when the credential-less request to `/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/secrets` returns HTTP 401 and the response body attributes no identity, AND — where component configuration is readable — every kube-apiserver instance carries `--anonymous-auth=false`, or an AuthenticationConfiguration whose `anonymous.enabled` is false, or whose `anonymous.conditions` list only `/healthz`, `/livez` and `/readyz`, AND the only binding naming `system:anonymous` or `system:unauthenticated` anywhere in the cluster is the built-in `system:public-info-viewer`. A 403 whose body names `system:anonymous`, a readable `--anonymous-auth=true`, an absent flag on a version whose documented default is true, or any additional binding to those subjects, is FAIL. Where the endpoint is unreachable from the assessment vantage and the component configuration is not readable, the verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW; an empty kube-apiserver pod list means unreadable and is never a PASS.
controls.remediation: On a self-managed control plane set `--anonymous-auth=false` in the kube-apiserver static pod manifest at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml; the kubelet restarts the pod when the file changes. Where an unauthenticated load balancer probe depends on /healthz, keep anonymous access narrowed rather than global by moving to the structured `--authentication-config` file and an AuthenticationConfiguration whose `anonymous` block enables only the conditions `/healthz`, `/livez` and `/readyz` (configurable anonymous endpoints reached beta in v1.32; on earlier versions the flag is all-or-nothing and the network restriction carries the risk instead). On a managed control plane where the setting is fixed by the provider, remove every RBAC binding that grants `system:anonymous` or `system:unauthenticated` anything beyond the built-in `system:public-info-viewer`, and put the API server endpoint behind the network restriction of control 1.12 so the anonymous identity is not reachable from the internet.
controls.caveat: Four false passes. First, a 403 reads like a refusal but proves the opposite of what is wanted: the request was authenticated as `system:anonymous` and only RBAC stopped it, so a collector that treats any non-200 as clean inverts the finding. Second, on AKS, EKS, GKE and OKE the API server does not run as a pod inside your cluster, so the label selector returns an empty list — that is unreadable, not absent, and unreadable maps to REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW for the configuration half while the unauthenticated HTTP probe still settles the behaviour; several managed distributions historically leave anonymous authentication on and rely wholly on RBAC, which makes the binding enumeration the substantive part of the assessment there. Third, `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=...` needs `impersonate` on users and groups; a permission error that prints nothing looks identical to an anonymous identity with no rules, so the exit status and stderr must be recorded with the output. Fourth, the binding sweep cuts both ways: `system:public-info-viewer` is bound to `system:unauthenticated` on every stock cluster, so a check that flags any such binding produces a finding on every healthy cluster, while a check that ignores all of them misses the one added grant this control exists to catch — the rule must be an explicit allow-list of that one built-in binding. Finally, RoleBindings are namespaced: a sweep without `--all-namespaces` reads only the namespace named by the kubeconfig context and reports a cluster clean on the strength of one namespace.

controls.title: Every authenticated request is authorised by RBAC and the node authoriser, never blanket-allowed
controls.objective: An authorization chain containing AlwaysAllow reduces the cluster to authentication only: any principal that can present a valid token can do anything, and no RBAC object written afterwards has any effect. The Node authoriser additionally confines each kubelet to the objects belonging to its own node, so that one compromised worker cannot read every secret in the cluster through the kubelet's own credential.
controls.procedure: Read `--authorization-mode` from the kube-apiserver command array, split it on commas and evaluate each element — the chain is a union, evaluated in order until an authorizer returns allow or deny, so a single AlwaysAllow anywhere in the list overrides every restriction expressed elsewhere. When the flag is absent, resolve what the default actually is rather than assuming a safe one: the kube-apiserver default for `--authorization-mode` is AlwaysAllow. From v1.29 the flag can be replaced by `--authorization-config` (beta in v1.30, stable in v1.32), which supersedes it with an AuthorizationConfiguration document listing typed authorizers in order; the two are mutually exclusive, so when the file is in use resolve it through the pod's `volumes` and `volumeMounts` and read the `authorizers` list, including any Webhook entry's `connectionInfo` and `failurePolicy`. Establish whether the Node authoriser is required here by looking at how kubelets authenticate: `kubectl --context <ctx> get csr` shows the bootstrap requests, and a `spec.username` of the form `system:node:<nodeName>` means node identities are in use and the Node authoriser belongs in the chain. Cross-check the chain behaviourally with an access review impersonating a principal that holds no bindings at all, `kubectl --context <ctx> auth can-i create pods --as=posture-probe@example.invalid -n kube-system`; under AlwaysAllow every such review answers yes. Where impersonation is not permitted to the assessor, submit a SubjectAccessReview object directly instead. Confirm the RBAC API is actually served, and on GKE confirm the legacy ABAC authoriser is off; on EKS also read `cluster.accessConfig.authenticationMode` and the access entries, because EKS access policies grant Kubernetes authority through a path that never appears as a ClusterRoleBinding.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.volumes[*]}'
kubectl --context <ctx> auth can-i create pods --as=posture-probe@example.invalid -n kube-system; echo "kubectl_exit=$?"
controls.evidence: The comma-separated value of `--authorization-mode`, or the full text of the AuthorizationConfiguration referenced by `--authorization-config` with its `authorizers` order preserved, quoted from the container command array and keyed by kube-apiserver pod name; the server version from `kubectl version -o json`, used to resolve what an absent flag means on that release; the `spec.username` values from CertificateSigningRequests showing whether kubelets present `system:node:<nodeName>` identities; the stdout answer and the stderr of the impersonated access review for a principal with no bindings; on GKE the value of `legacyAbac.enabled`; and on EKS the `authenticationMode` plus the list of access entries and the policies associated with each.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when the effective chain — the parsed elements of `--authorization-mode`, or the ordered `authorizers` of the file named by `--authorization-config` — contains an RBAC authorizer, contains a Node authorizer on any cluster where a CSR shows a `system:node:<nodeName>` requester, contains no `AlwaysAllow` element in any position, and the impersonated review for a principal holding no bindings prints `no` on stdout; and, where the cluster is GKE, `legacyAbac.enabled` is false. Both flags absent is FAIL, because the documented default is AlwaysAllow. `kubectl auth can-i` exits 1 for a denial and also exits 1 when impersonation itself is refused, so the exit code cannot decide this: the PASS token is the literal `no` on stdout, and an error on stderr is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW for that half. Where the control plane is managed and neither the flag nor the config file is readable, the probe printing `no` supports MET for the blanket-allow half only, and the presence of the Node authoriser is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW.
controls.remediation: Set `--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC` on every kube-apiserver instance and remove AlwaysAllow entirely; on v1.30 and later prefer the structured `--authorization-config` file so that authorizer ordering and any webhook's failure policy are explicit and versioned, and pair the Node authoriser with the NodeRestriction admission plugin of control 1.3, since the authoriser bounds what a kubelet may read and the plugin bounds what it may write. On GKE disable legacy ABAC with `gcloud container clusters update <cluster> --location <location> --no-enable-legacy-authorization`. On EKS, review every access entry and its associated access policies as part of the same review, since `AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy` grants cluster administration without any in-cluster object recording it. After the change, re-run the impersonated review for an unbound principal, confirm it prints `no`, then review the bindings previously masked by the permissive authoriser, because workloads may have depended on access they were never explicitly granted.
controls.caveat: The chain is a union, so asserting only that RBAC is present passes `RBAC,AlwaysAllow`, which is exactly as permissive as AlwaysAllow alone — parse every element, never substring-match for RBAC. An absent flag is the second trap and it cuts the opposite way from a flag whose default is safe: here absence means the permissive default, so a collector that treats a missing flag as inherited-and-fine records a wide-open cluster as compliant. On v1.30 and later a cluster may legitimately carry no `--authorization-mode` because `--authorization-config` replaced it, and reading only the flag then produces the same error in reverse, so check for both before concluding either way. Third, the impersonated probe needs `impersonate` on users; because `kubectl auth can-i` exits 1 both when the cluster denies and when the assessor may not impersonate, a collector keying on the exit code records its own missing permission as evidence that the cluster's authoriser is restrictive — the strongest false pass in this control. Fourth, a Webhook authorizer in the chain can return allow for everything while the flags read as ideal; resolve its endpoint, its `failurePolicy` and, in structured config, its match conditions before calling the chain restrictive. Fifth, on EKS with `authenticationMode` set to API or API_AND_CONFIG_MAP, cluster-admin is granted through access entries and access policies that no ClusterRoleBinding enumeration will ever show, so an RBAC-only review of that cluster is blind to its most privileged grants.

controls.title: Admission control enforces node isolation and a baseline pod security standard across every namespace
controls.objective: Admission is the last point at which the cluster can refuse a dangerous object. Without NodeRestriction a compromised kubelet can edit other node objects and label itself into another zone's workloads; without an enforcing Pod Security Admission level a workload can request host namespaces, privileged containers or hostPath mounts and convert a container compromise into node root. Both must be enforced by the API server, not by a linter in a pipeline that an attacker with API access bypasses entirely.
controls.procedure: Read `--enable-admission-plugins` and `--disable-admission-plugins` from the kube-apiserver command array. Interpret them carefully: most plugins are on by default and are named only when disabled, but NodeRestriction is not in the default set and is active only when explicitly enabled, while PodSecurity is in the default set from v1.25 and matters only if it has not been disabled. If `--admission-control-config-file` is set, resolve it through the pod's volumes and read the PodSecurityConfiguration it carries — both its `defaults`, which set the cluster-wide fallback level, and its `exemptions`, which disapply enforcement entirely for the listed namespaces, usernames and runtime classes regardless of any label. Pod Security Admission is otherwise driven by namespace labels; namespaces are cluster-scoped while the workloads they govern are namespaced, so enumerate every namespace and read `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce` on each, and separately list the namespaces that actually contain pods, because a check of the namespaces you happen to be working in says nothing about the rest of the cluster. Then prove enforcement rather than infer it: submit a deliberately privileged bare Pod with server-side dry-run, `kubectl --context <ctx> -n <representative-ns> apply --dry-run=server -f privileged-probe-pod.yaml`, which runs the whole admission chain including webhooks and validating admission policies without persisting anything. Enumerate the webhook and policy surface as well, recording each webhook's `failurePolicy`, `namespaceSelector`, `objectSelector` and `sideEffects`, and each ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding's `validationActions`. Finally inventory the workloads that already run with host namespaces or privilege, since those are what an enforcing level would have refused.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '[.items[].metadata.namespace] | unique[]'

kubectl --context <ctx> get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] as $c | $c.webhooks[] | "\($c.metadata.name)\t\(.name)\tfailurePolicy=\(.failurePolicy // "Fail")\tsideEffects=\(.sideEffects)\tnsSelector=\(.namespaceSelector // {})"'

kubectl --context <ctx> get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.hostPID==true or .spec.hostIPC==true or .spec.hostNetwork==true or any(.spec.volumes[]?; has("hostPath")) or any((.spec.containers[]?, .spec.initContainers[]?); .securityContext.privileged==true)) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'
controls.evidence: The values of `--enable-admission-plugins`, `--disable-admission-plugins` and `--admission-control-config-file` quoted from the kube-apiserver command array; the resolved PodSecurityConfiguration with both its `defaults` and its `exemptions` reproduced; the full namespace-to-enforce-label table covering every namespace in the cluster, alongside the list of namespaces that actually contain pods; the verbatim rejection message, or the successful creation output, from the server-side dry-run of the privileged probe Pod, with the namespace it was submitted to; the name, `failurePolicy`, `sideEffects`, `namespaceSelector` and `objectSelector` of every ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and the `validationActions` of every ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding that claims to enforce workload security; and the inventory of pods already running with host namespaces, hostPath volumes or privileged containers.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when NodeRestriction appears in `--enable-admission-plugins`, no `AlwaysAdmit` plugin appears anywhere, PodSecurity does not appear in `--disable-admission-plugins`, the effective enforce level of every namespace that contains at least one pod — the `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce` label where present, otherwise the `defaults.enforce` of the PodSecurityConfiguration — is `baseline` or `restricted`, no namespace containing pods appears in `exemptions.namespaces`, and the server-side dry-run of a privileged bare Pod in a representative namespace is rejected with a message naming the violated policy. Where the control-plane flags are unreadable, a dry-run rejection supports MET for the enforcement half while NodeRestriction is recorded REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW. A dry-run that succeeds is FAIL regardless of what the labels say. A dry-run that errors because a webhook declares it does not support dry-run is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, not a rejection.
controls.remediation: Add NodeRestriction to `--enable-admission-plugins` on every API server instance, alongside the Node authoriser of control 1.2. Label namespaces to enforce a standard, `kubectl label namespace <ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=<minor>`, rolling out with the `warn` and `audit` labels first so violations surface before they block. Set a cluster-wide fallback in an AdmissionConfiguration file referenced by `--admission-control-config-file`, so a namespace created tomorrow is not born unenforced, and keep its `exemptions` list empty or minimal and reviewed. On a managed control plane where the plugin list is not yours, achieve the equivalent with a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy whose binding sets `validationActions: [Deny]`, or an enforcing webhook with `failurePolicy: Fail`; on AKS use the built-in Azure Policy add-on rather than an unmanaged webhook.
controls.caveat: The default-on plugin set is the first trap: a name missing from `--enable-admission-plugins` usually means the plugin is on, but NodeRestriction is the exception and its absence means it is off — one rule cannot be applied to both. The second is namespace scope: workloads are namespaced, and a check that reads labels for the context's current namespace only, or that skips namespaces created after the rollout, reports a cluster as governed when most of it is not; kube-system is exempted in almost every rollout and is precisely where privileged workloads live. Third, the PodSecurityConfiguration `exemptions` block silently defeats the labels — a namespace, a username or a runtime class listed there is unenforced even with `enforce=restricted` on it, and if the assessor's own username is exempt the probe pod is admitted and the whole control reads as failing when it is not, or a genuinely exempt production namespace reads as enforced when it is not. Fourth, `warn` and `audit` labels are not enforcement: a namespace labelled only `pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted` emits a warning and admits the pod, so a collector matching on any `pod-security.kubernetes.io/*` label passes an unenforced cluster. Fifth, the probe object must be a bare Pod: Pod Security Admission enforces on pod creation, so dry-running a Deployment returns only a warning while the Deployment itself is accepted, and reading that acceptance as a pass inverts the result. Sixth, a webhook with `failurePolicy: Ignore`, a `namespaceSelector` that excludes the busy namespaces, or backing pods that are down enforces nothing while listing as present; conversely a webhook declaring `sideEffects: Unknown` causes the server to reject the dry-run request itself, which must not be recorded as a policy rejection. Seventh, on AKS, EKS, GKE and OKE the API server pod is not visible, so the plugin list is unreadable and must be reported as such rather than as absent.

controls.title: The API server records an audit event for every security-relevant request
controls.objective: The API server audit stream is the only artifact that ties a change in the cluster to the principal that made it. Without an audit policy in force there is no record of who read the secrets, who created the privileged pod, or which token was used, and an incident cannot be reconstructed at all. The policy must record at least metadata for every request while deliberately not recording the bodies of secret reads.
controls.procedure: Read `--audit-policy-file`, `--audit-log-path`, `--audit-log-maxage`, `--audit-log-maxbackup`, `--audit-log-maxsize` and `--audit-webhook-config-file` from the kube-apiserver command array, then resolve the policy file to the host path behind it using the pod's `volumes` and `volumeMounts` and read the document. It must be an `audit.k8s.io/v1` Policy. Rules are evaluated in order and the first match wins, so read it top down: a catch-all `level: None` near the top disables everything below it, and the terminal rule should be at least `level: Metadata`. Check specifically that requests against `secrets`, `configmaps` and the `serviceaccounts/token` subresource are recorded at Metadata level and not at Request or RequestResponse, since the latter two write the credential material itself into the log. On a managed control plane the flags are not visible and the audit stream is a provider feature, so read the enabled log categories from the provider API instead — and on GKE remember that Kubernetes read operations are Data Access logs, which are off by default and configured in the project IAM policy's `auditConfigs`, not in the cluster. Close the loop behaviourally: make one benign authorised call of your own carrying a nonce that will appear in the recorded request URI, for example a label selector `posture-probe=<nonce>`, then retrieve that exact record from the sink. That single retrieval is what separates a configured pipeline from a working one.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.volumes[*]}'

gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.serviceName="k8s.io" AND resource.labels.cluster_name="<cluster>" AND protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerSuppliedUserAgent!=""' --project <project> --freshness=1h --limit 5 --format json
controls.evidence: The verbatim audit flags from the kube-apiserver command array; the full text of the `audit.k8s.io/v1` Policy resolved from `--audit-policy-file`, with rule order preserved because the first matching rule decides the level, and with the levels applied to `secrets`, `configmaps` and `serviceaccounts/token` called out explicitly; on a managed control plane the provider's enabled audit categories (`cluster.logging.clusterLogging` for EKS, the diagnostic-setting categories for AKS, the project `auditConfigs` for GKE, and for OKE a statement of which stream was available); and the single audit record corresponding to the assessor's own nonce-bearing call, quoted from the sink together with the query that retrieved it and the clock time of the originating request.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when all three hold: an audit policy is in force — either a `--audit-policy-file` whose document contains no unqualified catch-all at `level: None` and whose terminal rule is at least `Metadata`, or the provider's Kubernetes audit category enabled on a managed control plane; a sink is configured — `--audit-log-path`, `--audit-webhook-config-file`, or the provider's log destination; and the assessor's nonce-bearing test call is retrievable from that sink. Any one of the three missing is FAIL. A policy that records `secrets` or `serviceaccounts/token` at Request or RequestResponse level is also FAIL, for disclosure rather than for absence. Where neither the flags nor a provider audit category can be read, the verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW; where the provider category is readable and reports disabled, that is FAIL, not unknown.
controls.remediation: Write an `audit.k8s.io/v1` Policy that drops only high-volume, low-value traffic by explicit user and resource (kubelet and kube-proxy read loops, /healthz, /version), records create, update, patch and delete at RequestResponse for workload and RBAC resources, records `secrets`, `configmaps` and token requests at Metadata only, and ends with a catch-all Metadata rule. Reference it with `--audit-policy-file` and set `--audit-log-path` with rotation flags, or forward directly with `--audit-webhook-config-file`. On EKS enable the audit log type, `aws eks update-cluster-config --name <cluster> --logging '{"clusterLogging":[{"types":["audit","authenticator"],"enabled":true}]}'`. On AKS add a diagnostic setting emitting the kube-audit categories to a workspace, choosing kube-audit-admin where read volume is the obstacle and recording that reads are then not captured. On GKE enable Data Access audit logs for `container.googleapis.com` in the project IAM policy, since Admin Activity logging alone omits reads.
controls.caveat: `--audit-log-path` without `--audit-policy-file` writes nothing at all, so a check that accepts either flag passes a cluster with no audit trail whatsoever. Rule ordering is the second trap: policies are frequently copied with a broad `level: None` exclusion near the top, intended for one noisy component but written without a user or resource qualifier, which silently discards every event beneath it while the file still reads as a full policy. Third, on AKS, EKS, GKE and OKE the flags cannot be read at all — an empty flag read must route to the provider query and never to a pass — and the provider defaults differ in a way that decides the verdict: on EKS the audit log type is off by default, so absence there is a genuine FAIL, whereas on GKE Admin Activity logging is always on and only Data Access logging is off, so a cluster can be partially covered while a naive query finds records and calls it complete. For OKE, OCI Audit records management-plane calls against the container engine API and is not the in-cluster Kubernetes API audit stream; treating one as the other is a false pass, and where no Kubernetes audit stream is exposed the verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW. Fourth, retrieving your own nonce-bearing event is what distinguishes a configured pipeline from a working one: a policy and a path can both be present while the disk is full, the webhook endpoint is refusing connections, or the log group was deleted. Fifth, over-collection is a real finding in the other direction — RequestResponse on secrets copies every secret value into a log whose readership is far wider than etcd's.

controls.title: Audit records outlive the node that produced them and cover the investigation window
controls.objective: An audit trail written only to the control-plane node's local disk is erased by the same node root compromise it is supposed to evidence, and one rotated away after a few hours cannot answer a question asked weeks later, which is when intrusions are usually noticed. The records must be held somewhere the cluster's own administrators and any attacker on the node cannot silently truncate, for at least the organisation's stated retention window.
controls.procedure: Read the rotation flags from the kube-apiserver command array and compute the retained volume rather than trusting the age setting: `--audit-log-maxbackup` files of `--audit-log-maxsize` MiB each is the hard ceiling, and `--audit-log-maxage` only bounds what has not already been rotated out beneath it. Compare that ceiling with the observed daily audit volume on a control-plane node. Establish whether the records leave the node at all: look for a shipping agent DaemonSet and for `--audit-webhook-config-file`. Then verify the destination rather than the agent by querying the sink itself for a record older than the window's start. For managed clusters read the retention of the provider's log store — the CloudWatch log group for EKS, the Log Analytics workspace behind the AKS diagnostic setting, the Cloud Logging buckets for GKE (both `_Required`, which holds Admin Activity for a fixed 400 days and cannot be shortened or lengthened, and `_Default`, which holds Data Access at 30 days unless changed), and OCI Audit for OKE. Separately establish who may delete from that store, because retention that the cluster's own administrators can erase does not survive the insider case this control exists for. Where the cluster is younger than the required window, the configured retention on the sink is the evidence and the age of the oldest retrievable record is recorded as a limitation.
api: az monitor log-analytics workspace show -g <resource_group> -n <workspace> --query '{retention:retentionInDays,capping:workspaceCapping,immediatePurge:features.immediatePurgeDataOn30Days}' -o json
controls.evidence: The computed retention ceiling for node-local logs — `--audit-log-maxbackup` multiplied by `--audit-log-maxsize`, alongside `--audit-log-maxage` — with the observed daily audit volume that makes it meaningful; the identity of the off-node sink and its configured retention (`retentionInDays` for a CloudWatch log group, the workspace retention for AKS, the `retentionDays` and `locked` state of the GKE `_Required` and `_Default` buckets); the timestamp of the oldest audit record actually retrievable from that sink, captured with the query that produced it; and the identity of the principals that hold delete or purge rights over the store.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when audit records are held in a store outside the control-plane node's local filesystem, the configured retention on that store is at least the organisation's stated window (90 days where none is stated), and a query against the store returns a record from the start of that window — or, for a cluster younger than the window, returns the earliest record in the cluster's lifetime with the configured retention evidencing the remainder. Node-local logs only, or a sink whose configured retention is shorter than the window, is FAIL. A shipping agent running with no record confirmed in the destination is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, never MET.
controls.remediation: Ship audit events off the node: use `--audit-webhook-config-file` to a collector, or a log agent reading the audit file, and give the destination an explicit retention. Set that retention deliberately rather than leaving the default — `aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /aws/eks/<cluster>/cluster --retention-in-days 365`, a workspace retention for the AKS diagnostic setting, a Cloud Logging bucket retention for GKE with the bucket locked where the window is a compliance obligation. Keep the node-local file as a short buffer sized to survive a collector outage rather than as the system of record, and scope write and delete rights on the destination so that a cluster administrator cannot remove their own trail.
controls.caveat: Marked Manual because the required window is an organisational and regulatory judgement, not an API fact: 90 days is a common floor, a regulated environment may need a year or more, and no API call can tell you which obligation applies to this cluster, whether the retention was set against that obligation, or whether the people who can purge the store are the same people the trail is meant to hold accountable. A human must read the retention requirement, confirm the sink implements it, and confirm the separation of duties over deletion. Four specific traps behind that judgement. Volume-based rotation makes `--audit-log-maxage` an upper bound and never a guarantee: a busy cluster rolls through `maxbackup` files in hours while the age setting still reads 30 days. The presence of a log-shipping DaemonSet is not delivery — it is common to find the agent running and healthy while the destination has been rejecting its writes for weeks, so a record actually retrieved from the sink is the only evidence. Node-local logs sit within reach of anyone with node root or a hostPath mount, so an attacker's cleanup is invisible while the configuration still reads as compliant. And a provider log group with no retention set never expires, which satisfies this control while creating an unbounded cost and an unbounded data-retention exposure that belong in the report as a separate observation.

controls.title: Secrets are written to etcd as ciphertext and pre-existing secrets have been rewritten
controls.objective: Objects in etcd are stored as the API server sends them, so without an encryption provider every Secret is plaintext in the etcd data directory, in every etcd snapshot and on every backup medium those snapshots reach. Anyone who obtains a backup, a detached disk or read access to the etcd data path then holds the cluster's credentials without ever touching the API server or leaving an audit record.
controls.procedure: Read `--encryption-provider-config` and `--encryption-provider-config-automatic-reload` from the kube-apiserver command array, resolve the file through the pod's volumes and read the `apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1` EncryptionConfiguration. For each entry in `resources`, the ordering of `providers` is what decides the outcome: the first provider listed is the one used to write, so an `identity` entry first means writes are plaintext even though a real provider sits below it. Confirm `secrets` appears in the resource list, and note whether `configmaps` does. Then prove it against the stored bytes rather than the configuration: from a control-plane node read a Secret straight out of etcd with the client certificates, `etcdctl get /registry/secrets/<namespace>/<name>`, piping the value through a hex dump because the stored object is binary, and check whether it begins with an encryption prefix such as `k8s:enc:kms:v2:` or `k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:` or whether the plaintext object header is visible. Count what is at stake with a cluster-wide Secret enumeration, which must carry `--all-namespaces` because Secrets are namespaced, and compare each Secret's `creationTimestamp` with the modification time of the encryption configuration — that comparison, not the configuration, is what shows whether the existing objects were ever rewritten. On a managed control plane neither the flag nor etcd is reachable, so read the provider's envelope-encryption state instead.
controls.evidence: The `--encryption-provider-config` flag and the full EncryptionConfiguration document with the provider ordering preserved for each resource type; the hex dump of the raw bytes returned by the etcd read of at least one Secret, showing either an encryption prefix or the plaintext object; the count and `creationTimestamp` of Secrets across all namespaces set against the modification time of the encryption configuration, which is what evidences whether pre-existing objects were rewritten; and on a managed control plane the provider's envelope-encryption fields — `cluster.encryptionConfig` for EKS, `databaseEncryption.state` with `keyName` for GKE, `securityProfile.azureKeyVaultKms` for AKS, the KMS key OCID for OKE.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when the effective EncryptionConfiguration lists a non-`identity` provider first for the `secrets` resource, AND a Secret sampled directly from etcd carries a `k8s:enc:` prefix rather than a readable object header, AND no Secret has a `creationTimestamp` earlier than the modification time of the encryption configuration without evidence of a rewrite. On a managed control plane, PASS when the provider reports envelope encryption enabled against a named key (`cluster.encryptionConfig` non-empty for EKS, `databaseEncryption.state` equal to ENCRYPTED with a `keyName` for GKE, `securityProfile.azureKeyVaultKms.enabled` true for AKS, a non-null KMS key OCID for OKE). `identity` first, or the flag absent with no provider-side envelope encryption, is FAIL. A correct configuration with Secrets predating it and no rewrite performed is PARTIALLY_MET. Where etcd cannot be read and the provider exposes no encryption field, the ciphertext half is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW and must not be inferred from the configuration alone.
controls.remediation: Add an `apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1` EncryptionConfiguration listing a KMS v2 provider first for `secrets` (and for `configmaps` where they hold sensitive values), reference it with `--encryption-provider-config`, and set `--encryption-provider-config-automatic-reload` so key rotation does not require a restart. Then rewrite every existing object so it is stored under the new provider, `kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -`, and re-sample etcd afterwards to confirm the rewrite landed. Where a local provider is unavoidable, keep its key material off the etcd host. On EKS enable envelope encryption with `aws eks associate-encryption-config --cluster-name <cluster> --encryption-config '[{"provider":{"keyArn":"<kms_key_arn>"},"resources":["secrets"]}]'`; on GKE use `gcloud container clusters update <cluster> --location <location> --database-encryption-key <key>`; on AKS enable the Key Vault KMS provider.
controls.caveat: The decisive false pass is that enabling a provider encrypts only objects written afterwards: every Secret created before the change stays plaintext in etcd indefinitely, so a configuration-only check passes a cluster whose entire credential store is readable from any backup — the rewrite, and the creation timestamps that prove it, are the substance of this control. Second, provider ordering: an `identity` entry first in the `providers` list is a valid configuration that writes plaintext while the file superficially reads as encrypted, so matching on the presence of a kms or aescbc block anywhere in the document is not enough. Third, `resources` typically names only `secrets`, leaving ConfigMaps that hold credentials untouched, and a wildcard entry can silently reorder what is covered. Fourth, a locally keyed aescbc or secretbox provider stores its key in a file on the same control-plane node as the etcd data directory, so it defends against a stolen snapshot or a detached disk and not at all against node root — it must not be reported as equivalent to a KMS provider. Fifth, on EKS the absence of `encryptionConfig` does not mean nothing is encrypted: the underlying storage is encrypted by the provider, which is disk-level and not envelope encryption of Secrets, and reading that as a pass is the most common managed-cluster error in this control. Sixth, the etcd read needs control-plane node access and a client certificate with clientAuth; a connection refused or a permission error is unreadable and maps to REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, never to a pass by absence of visible plaintext.

controls.title: etcd accepts only mutually authenticated TLS from the API server and from its own peers
controls.objective: etcd holds the entire cluster state, including every Secret and every RBAC object, and it applies no authorisation model of its own beyond the client certificate it demands. A client that can complete a TLS handshake to port 2379 and issue a request without presenting a trusted certificate can read and write the whole cluster invisibly to the API server audit log; a peer port that accepts unauthenticated connections lets an attacker join the raft cluster and rewrite the same data.
controls.procedure: Establish first whether the control plane is yours to read: `kubectl --context <ctx> get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane -o name` returning nothing, together with an empty etcd pod list, means the control plane is provider-operated and the flags do not exist for you to read. Where control-plane nodes are visible, read the etcd member flags from the mirrored static pods with `kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.nodeName}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'`, reading `command` and `args` together because a manifest that carries its flags in `args` yields an empty string from a `command`-only read, and every 'flag is absent' test then succeeds for free. Confirm the whole client set (`--cert-file`, `--key-file`, `--trusted-ca-file`, `--client-cert-auth=true`) and the whole peer set (`--peer-cert-file`, `--peer-key-file`, `--peer-trusted-ca-file`, `--peer-client-cert-auth=true`). Verify `--auto-tls` and `--peer-auto-tls` are absent or false, since they mint self-signed certificates that encrypt without authenticating anyone. Read `--listen-client-urls` and `--listen-peer-urls` to see which interfaces are bound. Then read the API server's side of the same connection: `--etcd-servers` must be https and `--etcd-cafile`, `--etcd-certfile` and `--etcd-keyfile` must all be set. Enumerate the membership with `etcdctl member list` and repeat the flag read against every member, since a three-member cluster can be misconfigured on one node only. Finish with a reachability probe from an ordinary workload vantage inside the cluster network: a request to https://<etcd_ip>:2379/version carrying no client certificate must be rejected. Under TLS 1.3 the client-certificate requirement is enforced after the handshake completes, so a completed `openssl s_client` handshake is not evidence of anything — send the request and record the rejection or the TLS alert.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=etcd -o wide

kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=etcd -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.nodeName}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'
controls.evidence: The complete etcd container `command` plus `args` arrays for every member pod, keyed by pod name and node, showing each of the eight client and peer TLS flags and the absence or false value of `--auto-tls` and `--peer-auto-tls`; the `etcdctl member list` table proving how many members were expected and how many were read; the `--etcd-servers`, `--etcd-cafile`, `--etcd-certfile` and `--etcd-keyfile` values from the kube-apiserver command array; and the transcript of the certificate-less request to port 2379 from a non-control-plane vantage, including the HTTP status or the TLS alert the server returned.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when the `command` and `args` arrays of every member returned by `etcdctl member list` carry `--cert-file`, `--key-file`, `--trusted-ca-file` and `--client-cert-auth=true`, plus `--peer-cert-file`, `--peer-key-file`, `--peer-trusted-ca-file` and `--peer-client-cert-auth=true`, with `--auto-tls` and `--peer-auto-tls` absent or set to false; the API server reaches etcd over https with all three etcd client credential flags set; and a request to port 2379 carrying no client certificate, sent from outside the control plane, is rejected rather than answered. Members enumerated but not read are REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW and cap the control at PARTIALLY_MET. On a managed control plane etcd is operated entirely by the provider and none of this is readable or changeable by the customer: the verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW evidenced by the provider's shared-responsibility documentation, and never MET by assumption.
controls.remediation: Set the four client-facing and four peer-facing TLS flags on every etcd member in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml and remove `--auto-tls` and `--peer-auto-tls`. Bind `--listen-client-urls` to the loopback and the control-plane interface only, never to a general-purpose network, and enforce that with a host firewall so mutual TLS is not the only barrier. Issue etcd server, peer and client certificates from a CA used for nothing else, so that a certificate trusted elsewhere in the estate cannot be replayed against etcd. Rotate the API server's etcd client certificate along with the rest of the control-plane PKI.
controls.caveat: Four concrete false passes live here. First, reading only `.spec.containers[*].command`: distributions that put flags in `args` return an empty command string, and a collector testing for the absence of `--auto-tls` scores that empty string as compliant — read both arrays and record their length. Second, `--auto-tls` itself: the connection is encrypted, a TLS scanner reports the port secured, and the server authenticates no client whatsoever. Third, the handshake probe under TLS 1.3, where client-certificate enforcement is deferred until after the handshake, so `openssl s_client` printing a completed handshake and a session ticket proves nothing; only a rejected request does. Fourth, the pod read itself: `component=etcd` in kube-system is a kubeadm convention, and k3s or RKE2 embedded etcd, OpenShift's `openshift-etcd` namespace, and etcd run as a systemd unit or as an external cluster all return an empty list, which is unreadable rather than compliant. Beyond the false passes, `--client-cert-auth=true` without `--trusted-ca-file`, or with a CA that also signs workload or ingress certificates, verifies a signature and proves nothing about who is calling — check what the CA signs, not merely that one is named. And read the finding together with control 1.6: unauthenticated etcd plus unencrypted secrets is a total credential compromise that leaves no audit record at all.

controls.title: Every kubelet refuses anonymous callers and delegates authorisation to the API server
controls.objective: The kubelet API on port 10250 can list pods, read logs, and execute commands inside any container on its node. A kubelet that accepts anonymous requests, or that authorises with AlwaysAllow, turns anything with network access to a worker node into arbitrary code execution in every workload on it — bypassing the API server entirely, and therefore bypassing RBAC and the audit trail together.
controls.procedure: Assert your own access before drawing any conclusion: `kubectl --context <ctx> auth can-i get nodes/proxy` must return yes, or every configz read below fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the cluster's posture. Enumerate the whole fleet with `kubectl --context <ctx> get nodes -o wide`; node pools, self-managed groups and Windows nodes are configured independently, so one node's answer is not the cluster's. For each node read the kubelet's effective merged configuration through the API server proxy: `kubectl --context <ctx> get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz"`. This returns the configuration actually in force, combining the config file, the command-line flags and the defaults, which is what a read of /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml on one host does not. From the returned `kubeletconfig` object read `authentication.anonymous.enabled` (must be false), `authentication.webhook.enabled` (must be true, so bearer tokens are checked by TokenReview), `authentication.x509.clientCAFile` (must name the CA that signs the API server's kubelet client certificate) and `authorization.mode` (must be Webhook, never AlwaysAllow). Then confirm behaviourally from a vantage on the node network — a pod in the cluster is sufficient — that an unauthenticated request is rejected at authentication and not merely at authorisation: `curl -sk -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://<node_ip>:10250/pods` must return 401. A 403 means anonymous authentication succeeded and only RBAC declined, which is one permissive binding away from a 200. Close that loop by listing any binding that grants the anonymous identities anything at all, since kubelet authorisation is delegated to the API server: search every ClusterRoleBinding and RoleBinding for a subject named `system:anonymous` or for the group `system:unauthenticated`.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(any(.subjects[]?; .name=="system:anonymous" or .name=="system:unauthenticated")) | "\(.kind) \(.metadata.namespace // "-") \(.metadata.name) -> \(.roleRef.name)"'
controls.evidence: The result of the `auth can-i get nodes/proxy` precheck; for every node returned by `kubectl get nodes`, the four fields `authentication.anonymous.enabled`, `authentication.webhook.enabled`, `authentication.x509.clientCAFile` and `authorization.mode` extracted from that node's `/proxy/configz` response, recorded with the node name, its kubelet version and the timestamp, together with the count of nodes read against the count of nodes present; the HTTP status code and body of the unauthenticated request to port 10250 on each node address, taken from a vantage proven to reach the port; and the list of bindings, if any, naming `system:anonymous` or `system:unauthenticated`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, for every node in `kubectl get nodes`, the effective kubelet configuration reports `authentication.anonymous.enabled=false`, `authentication.webhook.enabled=true`, `authorization.mode="Webhook"` and a non-empty `authentication.x509.clientCAFile`; an unauthenticated request to https://<node>:10250/pods returns exactly 401; and no ClusterRoleBinding or RoleBinding names `system:anonymous` or the group `system:unauthenticated`. A 403 to the unauthenticated request is FAIL, because it shows the request was authenticated as the anonymous identity and stopped only by authorisation. A single node answering 200 is FAIL for the whole control. Any node whose configz cannot be retrieved is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW for that node and caps the control at PARTIALLY_MET.
controls.remediation: Set `authentication.anonymous.enabled: false`, `authentication.webhook.enabled: true`, `authentication.x509.clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt` and `authorization.mode: Webhook` in the kubelet configuration file on every node, and restart the kubelet. Roll the change through the node image or launch template rather than by hand, so a scaled-out or replaced node inherits it — a manually fixed node pool regresses at the next scale event. Delete any binding that grants `system:anonymous` or `system:unauthenticated` more than the discovery roles. Confirm the API server holds a client certificate signed by that CA (control 1.11), otherwise disabling anonymous access breaks log and exec traffic. Restrict port 10250 at the network layer to the control-plane addresses as a second barrier.
controls.caveat: The 401-versus-403 distinction is the false pass that matters: a checker that accepts 'anything but 200' records a 403 as hardened, when a 403 means the kubelet authenticated the caller as `system:anonymous` and delegated the refusal to RBAC — one over-broad binding to `system:unauthenticated`, or an authorisation webhook outage handled permissively, turns it into a 200. The second false pass is the configz read itself: it needs `nodes/proxy`, and an RBAC 403 parses to the same empty object as a clean answer, so a collector that maps any non-200 to 'anonymous not enabled' converts a permissions gap into a compliant report. Third, sampling: managed node groups, spot pools, Windows nodes and hand-built nodes each carry their own kubelet configuration, the misconfigured one is rarely first in the list, and the loop must therefore cover every node the API server knows about with the count reported. Fourth, configz is the merged effective configuration and is the right source, but evidence taken from /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml alone can disagree with it because a systemd unit flag overrides the file. Fifth, this control is entirely the customer's even on AKS, EKS, GKE and OKE, because the kubelets run on your nodes — a managed control plane is no excuse for skipping it. Sixth, a 401 on 10250 says nothing about the unauthenticated read-only port covered by control 1.10.

controls.title: Kubelet client and serving certificates rotate automatically before they expire
controls.objective: Kubelet credentials are long-lived by default and their expiry takes a node out of the cluster without warning, which is why operators issue them with multi-year lifetimes and stop tracking them. Automatic rotation keeps each node's client credential short-lived so a stolen kubelet key is useful only briefly, and gives each kubelet a CA-signed serving certificate so the API server can verify it rather than trusting whatever is presented on port 10250.
controls.procedure: For every node, read the effective kubelet configuration through `kubectl --context <ctx> get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz"` and record `rotateCertificates` (client credential rotation), `serverTLSBootstrap` (serving certificate requested through the CSR API rather than self-signed), and `tlsCertFile`/`tlsPrivateKeyFile`, since statically supplied serving files alongside `serverTLSBootstrap` is a contradictory configuration that must be reconciled against the certificate actually served. Enabling serving-certificate bootstrap without an approver is worse than leaving it off, so examine the CSR surface: `kubectl --context <ctx> get csr` grouped by `spec.signerName`. The `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet` signer is auto-approved by kube-controller-manager for requests coming from `system:bootstrappers` and from existing node identities; nothing in the control plane auto-approves `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving`, so a third-party approver must be present and must have issued. Read the signing configuration from the controller-manager container `command` and `args` — `--cluster-signing-cert-file`, `--cluster-signing-key-file` and `--cluster-signing-duration`, which bounds the lifetime of everything it issues. Finally look at the certificates actually being served rather than the files on disk: `openssl s_client -connect <node_ip>:10250` and `openssl s_client -connect <apiserver_host>:6443` piped through `openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer -subject` give the effective issuer and expiry, which is what a process that never reloaded a rotated file will contradict.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz" | jq '.kubeletconfig | {rotate:.rotateCertificates, serverBootstrap:.serverTLSBootstrap, tlsCertFile:.tlsCertFile, tlsKeyFile:.tlsPrivateKeyFile}'
kubectl --context <ctx> get csr -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.signerName=="kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving") | [.metadata.name, (.status.conditions // [] | map(.type) | join(","))] | @tsv'

kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-controller-manager -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'
controls.evidence: Per node, the `rotateCertificates`, `serverTLSBootstrap`, `tlsCertFile` and `tlsPrivateKeyFile` values from the effective kubelet configuration; the CSR table grouped by `spec.signerName` showing whether `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving` requests reach Approved and Issued or sit Pending; the `--cluster-signing-duration` value read from the kube-controller-manager `command` plus `args`; and the issuer, subject and notAfter dates of the certificates actually served on each node's port 10250 and on the API server endpoint, plus the `kubeadm certs check-expiration` table where node access exists.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every node's effective kubelet configuration sets `rotateCertificates: true` and `serverTLSBootstrap: true`, no `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving` CSR is in Pending, every serving certificate presented on port 10250 has an issuer distinct from its own subject and equal to the cluster CA rather than being self-signed, and no certificate presented by a kubelet or by the API server has a notAfter within 30 days of the assessment date. A node where `rotateCertificates` is true but the kubelet's client credential is an embedded `client-certificate-data` blob rather than a file path is FAIL, because rotation cannot occur. On a managed control plane the API server and control-plane CA lifecycle belongs to the provider and that half is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW; the kubelet half is still assessed and must pass on its own.
controls.remediation: Set `rotateCertificates: true` and `serverTLSBootstrap: true` in the kubelet configuration shipped through the node image or launch template, and make sure the kubelet's kubeconfig references a certificate file under /var/lib/kubelet/pki rather than embedding the credential inline, since only a file-backed credential can be replaced. Deploy an approver for the `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving` signer that validates the requested subject and SANs against the node object before approving, since blanket approval of that signer lets a compromised node request a certificate for another node's name. Set `--cluster-signing-duration` on kube-controller-manager to a short lifetime so rotation is exercised routinely rather than at a cliff, and alert on CSRs pending longer than a bootstrap window. Approve a stuck request explicitly with `kubectl certificate approve <csr>` only after checking its subject.
controls.caveat: Enabling `serverTLSBootstrap` with no approver in place is the trap that reads as hardening and behaves as an outage: the CSRs queue Pending, kubelets keep serving self-signed certificates, and `kubectl logs` and `kubectl exec` either break or continue over an unverified channel — the presence of the setting is not evidence that rotation happens. The mirror-image false pass is `rotateCertificates: true` on a node whose kubelet kubeconfig embeds `client-certificate-data` inline: the flag is set, the check is green, and no rotation is possible because there is no file to replace, so confirm that /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem exists and is recent. kube-controller-manager auto-approves the client signer and never the serving signer, so the two must be evaluated separately rather than inferred from one another. `kubectl get csr` only lists requests still inside the API server's retention window — roughly an hour after completion — so an empty list is evidence of neither rotation nor its absence, and the dates on the served certificates are the durable evidence. Files on disk can be rotated without the process reloading them, which is why the assessment reads the certificate off the live socket. And on a managed control plane the control-plane PKI is not visible at all: report it unassessed rather than inferring it from the endpoint certificate, which is frequently a provider load-balancer certificate and not the API server's own.

controls.title: No node serves cluster state on the unauthenticated kubelet port
controls.objective: The kubelet read-only port answers over plain HTTP with no authentication at all and returns the full pod specification of everything running on the node, including environment variables, mounted secret and configmap names, service account names and container images. It is the cheapest reconnaissance in a cluster, it is reachable from any pod on the network, and nothing it serves is logged by the API server.
controls.procedure: For every node in `kubectl --context <ctx> get nodes -o wide`, read the effective kubelet configuration through `kubectl --context <ctx> get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz"` and check `readOnlyPort`, which must be 0. configz always serialises the whole effective structure, so the field is present in that response whatever supplied it; only a read of a kubelet config file can omit it, and absence there is not evidence of 0, because the deprecated `--read-only-port` command-line flag overrides the file and the unset default has differed across kubelet versions and vendor node images, several of which shipped 10255. Resolve any such ambiguity against the kubelet version from `kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion}'`. Then confirm it on the wire from a vantage on the node network — a pod in the cluster is the right vantage — by requesting unauthenticated plain HTTP on every address the node advertises, not just its primary InternalIP: `curl -s --max-time 5 http://<node_ip>:10255/pods`, `/stats/summary` and `/metrics`. Use those paths specifically: the debugging handlers such as /runningpods/ and /exec are registered only on the authenticated listener, so probing them returns 404 even on a node whose read-only port is wide open. Where the kubelet predates 1.12, probe the standalone cAdvisor port 4194 the same way; it was removed from the kubelet in 1.12 and cannot be present afterwards. A connection refused from a vantage that is proven to reach port 10250 is meaningful; a timeout from a vantage that reaches nothing is not.
controls.evidence: The `readOnlyPort` value from every node's effective kubelet configuration together with that node's kubelet version; the HTTP status code and, where non-empty, the first bytes of the body returned by the unauthenticated plain-HTTP requests to /pods, /stats/summary and /metrics on port 10255 for each advertised node address; and the paired 401 from port 10250 on the same node from the same vantage, which is what makes a refusal on 10255 attributable to the kubelet rather than to the network path.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every node's effective kubelet configuration reports `readOnlyPort: 0`, and unauthenticated plain-HTTP requests to /pods, /stats/summary and /metrics on port 10255 are refused on every advertised address of every node, each from a vantage that returned 401 from port 10250 on that same node. Any node returning 200 with a body on 10255, or any node whose kubelet configuration reports a non-zero `readOnlyPort`, is FAIL. Nodes whose configz cannot be read and which cannot be probed from an in-network vantage are REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW and cap the control at PARTIALLY_MET.
controls.remediation: Set `readOnlyPort: 0` in the kubelet configuration and bake it into the node image or launch template so replacement nodes inherit it. Migrate anything that consumed the read-only port — old monitoring agents are the usual dependency — to the authenticated port 10250 with a service account granted `nodes/metrics` and `nodes/stats`, or to the metrics endpoint the API server proxies. Add a host firewall or security-group rule denying 10255 and 4194 from the pod network as a second barrier, so a regressed node image does not reopen the exposure silently.
controls.caveat: The probe vantage decides the answer, and that is where the first false pass lives: running the check from a workstation outside the node network gives connection refused for every port on every node, which reads exactly like a hardened fleet. Anchor each probe by first getting a 401 from port 10250 on the same node from the same place, and treat any node you cannot reach as unassessed. The second false pass is probing the wrong path: /runningpods/ and the exec handlers exist only on the authenticated listener, so they answer 404 on an exposed read-only port and a checker keyed to them declares the node clean — probe /pods, /stats/summary and /metrics instead. Third, nodes advertise more than one address and a kubelet can be bound on a secondary interface only, so iterate `.status.addresses` rather than the InternalIP alone. Fourth, an absent `readOnlyPort` in a kubelet config file is not the same as 0: the deprecated `--read-only-port` flag overrides the file, and the value assumed when nothing sets it has varied by kubelet version and by vendor node image, so only the merged configz value settles it. Fifth, node pools are configured independently, so one clean pool proves nothing about the next and a scale-out from an old launch template reintroduces the port after the assessment. Finally, the in-cluster probe pod itself can be refused by Pod Security admission or by a restrictive namespace policy — a failure to schedule it is an unassessed node, not a passing one.

controls.title: The API server authenticates to kubelets with a client certificate and verifies the certificate they present
controls.objective: Every `kubectl logs`, `exec`, `attach` and `port-forward` is proxied by the API server to the kubelet. Without `--kubelet-client-certificate` the API server arrives at the kubelet as an anonymous caller, which is only survivable because control 1.8 rejects it. Without `--kubelet-certificate-authority` the API server does not verify the kubelet's serving certificate at all, so anything able to answer on port 10250 — or to redirect traffic to it — can impersonate a node and capture the exec sessions and log streams of workloads on it.
controls.procedure: Read the API server container `command` and `args` together with `kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'` and confirm all three flags are present: `--kubelet-client-certificate`, `--kubelet-client-key` and `--kubelet-certificate-authority`. Resolve the CA path through the pod's `volumes` and `volumeMounts` to a host path, then establish that it is the CA which actually signs kubelet serving certificates rather than the generic cluster CA used for client authentication, by comparing its subject to the issuer of the certificate served on a node's port 10250 (`openssl s_client -connect <node_ip>:10250 </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer`). Where node access exists, read the client certificate's subject from the file the flag points at; where it does not, take the identity from the API server's own audit or authentication configuration and say which source was used. Resolve that identity to its bindings and confirm its kubelet API rights come from `system:kubelet-api-admin` and not from a broader cluster-wide role. This control depends on control 1.9: verifying kubelet serving certificates is only possible where `serverTLSBootstrap` has produced CA-signed certificates carrying correct SANs, so assess the two together.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.volumes[*]}'
controls.evidence: The `--kubelet-client-certificate`, `--kubelet-client-key` and `--kubelet-certificate-authority` flags, quoted from the kube-apiserver `command` plus `args` with their host paths resolved through the pod volumes; the subject and issuer of the client certificate at that path, with a note of whether it was read from the node or inferred; the full list of certificates contained in the file named by `--kubelet-certificate-authority`; the issuer and subjectAltName of the certificate actually served on port 10250 by a sampled node, which is what shows whether the configured CA can in fact verify it; and the list of subjects bound to `system:kubelet-api-admin`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when the kube-apiserver `command` plus `args` carry all three flags with non-empty values; the file named by `--kubelet-certificate-authority` contains a certificate whose subject equals the issuer of the certificate served on port 10250 by every sampled node; and the identity in `--kubelet-client-certificate` appears in no ClusterRoleBinding other than one referencing `system:kubelet-api-admin`. Any of the three flags absent is FAIL — a missing `--kubelet-certificate-authority` is the common case and means no verification is performed. On a managed control plane none of these flags is readable and no behavioural probe distinguishes the states, so the verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW backed by the provider's documentation; it is never MET by default.
controls.remediation: Add `--kubelet-certificate-authority=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt` alongside the existing `--kubelet-client-certificate` and `--kubelet-client-key` in the kube-apiserver manifest, but only after `serverTLSBootstrap` and an approver are in place on every node (control 1.9) and every kubelet serving certificate carries the node's hostname and IP as SANs — otherwise log and exec traffic fails cluster-wide the moment verification is enabled. Roll it out node pool by node pool, watching for verification failures in the API server log, and keep the kubelet client identity bound to `system:kubelet-api-admin` rather than to a broader role.
controls.caveat: The decisive point is that no behavioural test distinguishes a verifying API server from a non-verifying one: `kubectl logs` and `kubectl exec` succeed identically in both cases, so the smoke test in the call list only proves the path works and is not evidence for this control — only the flag settles it. That is what makes the control genuinely unanswerable from the customer side on AKS, EKS, GKE and OKE, where the honest verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW rather than an assumption that the provider does the right thing. The subtler false pass is a flag that is present but useless: `--kubelet-certificate-authority` pointed at a multi-certificate bundle, or at a CA that signs nothing on port 10250, satisfies a presence check while verifying against the wrong trust anchor, so enumerate the certificates in the file and match one subject to the live issuer instead of testing that the path is non-empty. Operationally, the flag is frequently left unset on purpose because enabling it breaks logs and exec on any node whose serving certificate is self-signed or lacks the right SANs — the absence therefore looks like an oversight but is usually an undocumented risk acceptance, and the report should say so. Reading the client certificate from /etc/kubernetes/pki needs node or SSH access that a purely API-based assessment does not have; where that is missing, record the identity as inferred rather than observed.

controls.title: The API server endpoint is reachable only from networks the operator has named
controls.objective: An API server published to the whole internet exposes the authentication surface, the token endpoints and every unauthenticated path to continuous credential-stuffing and to any future authentication bypass, and it makes stolen kubeconfig credentials usable from anywhere on earth. Restricting who can open a connection at all is the control that survives a mistake in authentication or authorisation, which is why it is worth having even when RBAC is sound.
controls.procedure: Resolve the endpoint the kubeconfig actually points at with `kubectl --context <ctx> config view --raw --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}'` and resolve its name to an address; an RFC1918 address is not by itself proof of restriction, and a public address is not by itself proof of exposure. Read the provider's access configuration, which is the authoritative statement: for AKS `az aks show --query 'apiServerAccessProfile'` gives `authorizedIpRanges` and `enablePrivateCluster`; for EKS `aws eks describe-cluster --query 'cluster.resourcesVpcConfig'` gives `endpointPublicAccess`, `endpointPrivateAccess` and `publicAccessCidrs`, the last of which is 0.0.0.0/0 unless it was set; for GKE read `privateClusterConfig` and `masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig`; for OKE read the cluster endpoint configuration and its network security groups. For a self-managed control plane, read the load balancer or security group in front of port 6443 instead. Then test from vantage rather than trusting the configuration alone: attempt a TCP connection to the endpoint from an address outside every listed range and from an address inside one, and record both results with the source address each attempt actually presented. Finally attempt the same connection from an ordinary workload pod, because a private endpoint remains reachable by everything in the VPC. Record, for each allowlisted CIDR, who owns it and how many hosts sit behind it — that attribution is the part of this control an API cannot produce and a human must supply in writing.
controls.evidence: The endpoint URL from the kubeconfig and the address it resolves to; the provider's access-configuration object as returned (`apiServerAccessProfile` for AKS, `resourcesVpcConfig` for EKS, `privateClusterConfig` plus `masterAuthorizedNetworksConfig` for GKE, the endpoint configuration for OKE) including every allowlisted CIDR; paired connection results from at least two vantages — one outside all listed ranges and one inside — each recorded with the source address the attempt presented, plus the result from an in-cluster pod; and a dated, named written statement from the operator identifying the owner and the approximate population of every allowlisted CIDR.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when either `enablePrivateCluster`/`enablePrivateEndpoint` is true with public access disabled, or public access is enabled with a non-empty allowlist containing neither 0.0.0.0/0 nor ::/0, in which every prefix shorter than /24 is individually named in the operator attestation; and a connection attempt from a vantage outside every listed range fails at the network layer while an attempt from inside a listed range reaches the endpoint; and the evidence carries a dated written attestation naming the owner of each allowlisted CIDR. A public endpoint whose allowlist is empty or contains an all-addresses prefix is FAIL. Missing attestation, unreadable provider configuration, or the absence of an off-network vantage each make the verdict REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW.
controls.remediation: Prefer a private endpoint and reach it over the operator's own connectivity. Where a public endpoint is required, set an allowlist and keep it to specific egress addresses: `az aks update -g <rg> -n <cluster> --api-server-authorized-ip-ranges <cidrs>`, `aws eks update-cluster-config --name <cluster> --resources-vpc-config endpointPublicAccess=true,publicAccessCidrs=<cidrs>,endpointPrivateAccess=true`, `gcloud container clusters update <cluster> --location <location> --enable-master-authorized-networks --master-authorized-networks <cidrs>`. Review the list on a schedule, because allowlists accumulate ranges for departed contractors and retired offices, and pair the restriction with the anonymous-access and authorisation controls rather than treating it as a substitute for them.
controls.caveat: Marked Manual because the API can list the allowlisted ranges but cannot judge them, and no query can settle ownership: a corporate VPN egress /16 shared with tens of thousands of users, a shared cloud NAT range through which every other workload in the account also egresses, or a CI vendor's published egress block is an allowlist in form and the public internet in substance. Only a human who knows the estate can attribute each range, which is why the attestation is required evidence rather than a nicety. Four concrete traps. On EKS `endpointPrivateAccess=true` does not disable public access — the two settings are independent, and the common misconfiguration is both enabled with `publicAccessCidrs` still 0.0.0.0/0, which several dashboards summarise as a private cluster. A private endpoint is reachable from every pod and every host in the VPC, so 'private' bounds the internet and not the blast radius of one compromised workload — probe from a pod and report the answer. A failed connection from your own vantage proves only that your vantage is blocked: without a paired attempt from inside an allowlisted range, a network fault, a DNS split-horizon answer or an egress proxy is indistinguishable from a working restriction, so record the source address each attempt actually presented. And an allowlist entry covering your own NAT gateway admits every other tenant of that gateway, which is why prefix length alone is not the measure.

controls.title: Controller manager and scheduler expose no profiling or debug surface beyond the control-plane host
controls.objective: The controller manager and scheduler serve /debug/pprof and /metrics on their own secure ports, and profiling output discloses memory contents, request paths and internal state while also giving any caller a cheap way to stall the process. Binding these components to the loopback interface and disabling profiling removes a debug surface that no workload has any reason to reach.
controls.procedure: Read the full argument vector for all three control-plane components, taking BOTH `.spec.containers[*].command` and `.spec.containers[*].args` — a distribution that packs flags into `args` while `command` holds only the binary path will otherwise read as 'flag absent'. Use `kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-controller-manager -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'` and the same for `component=kube-scheduler` and `component=kube-apiserver`.
