Assert the pod list is non-empty before drawing any conclusion, because an empty result is indistinguishable from a mistyped label selector or from a managed control plane. Check `--profiling` on all three: the flag defaults to true in every one of these binaries, so an absent flag fails this control rather than passing it. Check `--bind-address` on the controller manager and scheduler, which should be 127.0.0.1 so their secure ports 10257 and 10259 are not offered on a routable interface; the binary's own default is 0.0.0.0, and it is kubeadm-generated manifests that have written 127.0.0.1 since v1.22, so absence of the flag is not evidence either way and must be settled behaviourally. Resolve version-dependent flag availability against `kubectl version -o json`: the API server's `--insecure-port` and `--insecure-bind-address` were removed in v1.20, and the controller manager's and scheduler's legacy `--port`/`--address` were removed in v1.23, so assert on them only where the reported server version still accepts them. Then probe from another host on the control-plane network: request /debug/pprof/ on ports 10257, 10259 and on the API server's 6443, recording the curl exit status alongside the HTTP status so that a refused connection (exit 7) is distinguishable from an authenticated rejection (401/403). Finally verify the controller manager runs with `--use-service-account-credentials=true` so individual controllers act under their own service accounts rather than the controller manager's blanket identity.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-controller-manager -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-scheduler -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pods -l tier=control-plane -o json | jq -r '.items | length'
controls.evidence: The full container `command` AND `args` arrays of kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler and kube-apiserver, keyed by pod name and node, with the pod count recorded so that an empty read is distinguishable from a compliant one; the server version from `kubectl version -o json` used to decide which legacy flags are still assertable; and, per probed port (10257, 10259, 6443), both the HTTP status code and the curl exit status returned by an unauthenticated request to /debug/pprof/ issued from a host other than the control-plane node.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when the pod list for all three label selectors is non-empty AND the parsed argument vector (command plus args) shows `--profiling=false` on kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler, `--bind-address=127.0.0.1` on kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler, `--use-service-account-credentials=true` on kube-controller-manager, no legacy insecure-serving flag set to a non-zero or non-loopback value on any version that still accepts one, and the off-host probe of ports 10257 and 10259 returns curl exit 7 or 28 (no listener reachable) rather than any HTTP status. An absent `--profiling` flag is FAIL because the binary default enables it. An absent `--bind-address` is not by itself a verdict: it resolves to FAIL if the off-host probe returns any HTTP status code on 10257 or 10259, and to PASS on that sub-condition only if the probe cannot connect. Where any of the three pod lists is empty, the verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, never PASS.
controls.remediation: Add `--profiling=false` to the kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests, set `--bind-address=127.0.0.1` explicitly on the controller manager and scheduler rather than relying on the manifest generator having done so, and set `--use-service-account-credentials=true` on the controller manager so each controller carries its own identity and its actions are attributable in the audit log. Where a metrics collector scrapes 10257 or 10259, run it on the control-plane node or scrape through an authenticated proxy rather than reopening the bind address. On a managed control plane none of this is configurable and the argument vector is not readable through the API; the compensating control is that those ports are not exposed to the customer network at all — state that, and record the verdict as REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW rather than claiming the setting.
controls.caveat: Four traps. (1) Absent-means-unsafe: `--profiling` defaults to true, so a checker that only flags the literal `--profiling=true` and treats absence as inherited-safe passes every default installation. (2) The mirror-image error on `--bind-address`: the binary default is 0.0.0.0, and it is the kubeadm-generated manifest that has carried 127.0.0.1 since v1.22 — so neither 'absent means unsafe' nor 'absent means safe' is correct, and this sub-condition must be settled by the off-host probe. (3) Flags may live in `args` rather than `command`; reading only `command` yields an empty flag set that a naive rule scores either way. (4) The status-code probe does not prove profiling is disabled — the secure ports 10257/10259 and the API server's 6443 all sit behind delegated authentication and authorization, so an unauthenticated request returns 401/403 even when profiling is fully enabled; the flag is the authoritative evidence and the probe only measures network exposure, so record the port and both the HTTP status and the curl exit status with each result. The empty-result trap is acute because all three label selectors have the same shape: on AKS, EKS, GKE and OKE all three return nothing, and so does a typo, so assert a non-empty pod list and route the managed case to REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW.

controls.title: Service account tokens are audience-bound, time-limited and tied to a live account
controls.objective: A legacy service account token secret is a bearer credential with no expiry and no audience, valid for as long as the secret object exists and usable from anywhere the API server is reachable. Bound tokens issued through the TokenRequest API expire, name the audience they are valid for, and are invalidated when the pod or the service account behind them disappears, which turns a stolen token from a permanent foothold into a short-lived one.
controls.procedure: Read `--service-account-lookup`, `--service-account-key-file`, `--service-account-signing-key-file`, `--service-account-issuer`, `--api-audiences` and `--service-account-max-token-expiration` from the kube-apiserver argument vector, taking both `command` and `args`. Note that `--service-account-lookup` defaults to true, so its absence is acceptable here — the opposite of the profiling and authorization flags, which is exactly why an 'absent flag' rule cannot be applied uniformly across this section. On a managed control plane where the argument vector is unreadable, mint a token and read it instead, which works everywhere: `kubectl --context <ctx> -n <ns> create token <serviceaccount> --duration=10m --audience=<expected>`, then base64url-decode the JWT payload and read `iss`, `aud`, `iat`, `exp` and the `kubernetes.io` bound object reference. Compare `iss` byte-for-byte against the `issuer` field of the cluster's own discovery document at `/.well-known/openid-configuration`; a legacy or shared issuer string means a token from one cluster is replayable against another that trusts the same key. Then enumerate legacy token secrets across the whole cluster — Secrets are namespaced, so this MUST carry `--all-namespaces`; without it the command reads only the namespace the context selects and reports zero on a cluster holding hundreds. Finally establish which pods still receive a token at all, reading the mount decision from both levels: a pod with `automountServiceAccountToken` unset inherits the ServiceAccount's setting, so the pod list alone cannot answer it.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].command}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].args}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl --context <ctx> get serviceaccounts --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.secrets != null) | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, ([.secrets[].name] | join(","))] | @tsv'

kubectl --context <ctx> get serviceaccounts --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, (if .automountServiceAccountToken == null then "unset(inherits-default-true)" else (.automountServiceAccountToken|tostring) end)] | @tsv'

kubectl --context <ctx> get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, (.spec.serviceAccountName // "default"), (if .spec.automountServiceAccountToken == null then "unset(inherits-sa)" else (.spec.automountServiceAccountToken|tostring) end)] | @tsv'
controls.evidence: The service account flags quoted from the kube-apiserver `command` and `args` arrays where readable; the decoded header and payload of a token freshly minted with `kubectl create token`, showing `iss`, `aud`, `iat`, `exp` and the `kubernetes.io` bound object reference, retained with the exact minting command and timestamp; the `issuer` value returned by the cluster's `/.well-known/openid-configuration`; the full cross-namespace list of `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` secrets with their creation timestamps and owning service accounts; and the paired pod-level and ServiceAccount-level `automountServiceAccountToken` values that together determine whether each pod actually receives a token. Where token minting is refused, the verbatim 403 message is the evidence, recorded as an access limitation and not as a configuration result.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when ALL of: a freshly minted token decodes to a non-empty `aud` array containing the requested audience; `exp - iat` is less than or equal to the requested duration plus 60 seconds; `iss` is an https URL that string-equals the `issuer` field of the cluster's discovery document and is not the legacy value `kubernetes/serviceaccount`; `--service-account-lookup` is either absent or set to true; and `kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token` returns zero rows, or only rows whose namespace/name pair appears on a written exception list. A token with an empty `aud`, or with the legacy issuer, is FAIL. Any legacy token secret not on the exception list is at best PARTIALLY_MET. Where the kube-apiserver argument vector is unreadable AND token minting returns 403, the verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW rather than PASS.
controls.remediation: Set a cluster-unique `--service-account-issuer` (an https URL identifying this cluster), set `--api-audiences` to match, and leave `--service-account-lookup` at its default of true so tokens die with the account. Delete legacy token secrets once the workloads that used them have been moved to projected service account token volumes, confirming nothing still mounts them before deleting. Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount and on pods that make no API calls, so a compromised container has no token to steal at all. Where an external system needs a credential, issue it a bound token with an explicit audience through the TokenRequest API on a refresh schedule rather than handing it a static secret.
controls.caveat: The absent-flag rule inverts here: `--service-account-lookup` defaults to true, so its absence is fine, while an absent `--profiling` in 1.13 means the unsafe default — applying one convention across the section produces a wrong verdict in one direction or the other. The namespace trap is decisive: `kubectl get secrets --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token` without `--all-namespaces` inspects only the namespace the current context selects and returns zero on clusters full of legacy tokens. Automatic generation of those secrets stopped in v1.24, but ones created before an upgrade survive it untouched and keep working, so a check that reasons from the cluster version instead of from the objects misses them entirely. Token minting requires `create` on the `serviceaccounts/token` subresource; a 403 there is an access answer and must never be recorded as a configuration finding or allowed to collapse into PASS. The mount question needs both levels — a pod whose `automountServiceAccountToken` is unset inherits the ServiceAccount's value, so reading only the pod spec mislabels inheriting pods. And a bound token stays valid until `exp` even after its pod is deleted, so 'bound' shortens the theft window rather than closing it.

controls.title: Every workload-bearing namespace enforces a Pod Security Standard at admission, not merely warns
controls.objective: Pod Security Admission is the built-in gate that stops a privileged, host-namespace-sharing or host-path-mounting pod from ever being created. It is configured per namespace through labels, and only the enforce mode actually rejects; a namespace carrying only warn or audit labels admits exactly the same dangerous pod it complains about. Every namespace that can host workloads should enforce baseline at minimum and restricted wherever the workload does not have a documented need for more.
controls.procedure: Bind the context first: run `kubectl config current-context` and `kubectl --context <ctx> cluster-info`, confirm the API server URL matches the cluster in scope, then pass `--kubeconfig` and `--context` explicitly on every subsequent call so an ambient current-context cannot silently redirect the assessment at a different cluster. Record the server version (`kubectl --context <ctx> version -o json | jq -r .serverVersion.gitVersion`); the PodSecurity admission plugin has been enabled by default since v1.23 as beta and went stable in v1.25. Namespaces are cluster-scoped, so one listing covers the estate: dump every namespace with its enforce, enforce-version, warn and audit labels and record which are unset. Then prove enforcement empirically rather than trusting the label: write a probe manifest for a pod with `securityContext.privileged: true` and submit it into each namespace with `kubectl apply --dry-run=server`, which runs the admission chain without creating anything. Read the rejection message, do not merely count the non-zero exit: a PASS requires a message naming the policy (it contains `violates PodSecurity`), because the API server also rejects dry-run requests outright when a matching webhook declares `sideEffects: Unknown` or `Some`, and that failure is about dry-run support, not about pod security. Finally enumerate `validatingwebhookconfigurations` and `validatingadmissionpolicybindings` so that a cluster enforcing pod security through Kyverno, Gatekeeper or a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is credited rather than failed — checking, in each case, that it actually denies: a webhook needs `failurePolicy: Fail`, and a policy binding needs `Deny` in `spec.validationActions` rather than only `Warn` or `Audit`.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.name, ((.webhooks // []) | map(.name + ":" + (.failurePolicy // "Fail")) | join(","))] | @tsv'
kubectl --context <ctx> get validatingadmissionpolicybindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.name, (.spec.policyName // "-"), ((.spec.validationActions // ["Deny"]) | join(","))] | @tsv'
controls.evidence: The per-namespace label map from the `kubectl get namespaces -o json` dump, showing the literal value of the enforce, enforce-version, warn and audit labels for each namespace name; the verbatim API server response to the server-side dry-run of the privileged probe pod in each namespace, retained in full so the rejection reason (a PodSecurity violation versus a webhook that does not support dry-run) is readable from the evidence rather than inferred; and the names, `failurePolicy` values and `validationActions` of any admission webhooks or validating admission policy bindings offered as the equivalent control.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every namespace capable of hosting workloads carries `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce` set to `baseline` or `restricted`, carries an `enforce-version` pinned to a concrete version string rather than being unset or `latest`, AND the server-side dry-run of the privileged probe pod in each of those namespaces is rejected with a message containing the literal substring `violates PodSecurity`. A namespace whose only PSA labels are `warn` or `audit` is FAIL. A rejection whose message does not name a pod-security violation — in particular one stating that a webhook does not support dry run — does not count toward PASS and is recorded as an inconclusive probe. A cluster enforcing through admission machinery instead of PSA passes only when the probe is rejected in every workload namespace AND every webhook in the rejecting chain has `failurePolicy: Fail`, or every binding relied upon lists `Deny` in `spec.validationActions`.
controls.remediation: Label each namespace, for example `kubectl --context <ctx> label --overwrite namespace <ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.30 pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted`. Roll out in stages: set warn and audit first, read what would break from the warnings, then move enforce. On a self-managed control plane set a cluster-wide default in the AdmissionConfiguration file referenced by `--admission-control-config-file` so a newly created namespace is not born unenforced. Where a workload genuinely needs baseline rather than restricted, isolate it in its own namespace and record the exception.
controls.caveat: The label-presence check is the classic false pass: `warn` and `audit` emit a message and admit the pod anyway, so a namespace that greps as 'has PSA labels' can still be running privileged workloads — and the same warn-not-enforce trap recurs one level up, in a Kyverno/Gatekeeper webhook with `failurePolicy: Ignore` or a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding whose `validationActions` are `Warn`/`Audit` only, either of which produces a complaint and an admitted pod. The probe has its own false pass: the API server refuses dry-run requests when a matching webhook declares `sideEffects: Unknown` or `Some`, so a checker that scores any non-zero exit as 'rejected, therefore enforced' passes clusters with no pod-security control at all; require the `violates PodSecurity` text. `enforce` without `enforce-version` floats to the running version, so the policy silently tightens on upgrade and can begin rejecting production workloads — an unpinned version is a finding in its own direction. PSA can also be disabled globally or exempted for named namespaces, users and runtime classes in the AdmissionConfiguration file passed to the API server; that file lives on the control-plane host and on EKS, GKE or AKS is simply not reachable through the Kubernetes API, so on a managed cluster the labels alone are not proof and the server-side dry-run is the only obtainable evidence. Finally PSA evaluates pod creation only: pods already running when the label was applied keep running, and a Deployment is admitted even when the pods it wants are rejected (the failure surfaces on the ReplicaSet, not on the Deployment), so a correctly labelled namespace can still contain privileged pods and controls 2.2 to 2.7 must be assessed against live objects regardless of this verdict.

controls.title: No workload runs a privileged container or leaves privilege escalation open
controls.objective: A privileged container holds every Linux capability, an unmasked /proc and unrestricted device access; it is a root shell on the node behind an API object. `allowPrivilegeEscalation` left open lets a process gain more privileges than its parent through setuid binaries even in an otherwise unprivileged container. Both must be closed on every container in the cluster, with the small set of infrastructure agents that genuinely need privilege named as explicit, reviewed exceptions.
controls.procedure: Collect the whole estate in two passes, because neither pass alone is complete. First dump every live pod cluster-wide with `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json` — the `--all-namespaces` flag is not optional, since a call without it reads only the namespace baked into the selected context and reports a clean cluster from one namespace's worth of evidence. Walk `.spec.containers`, `.spec.initContainers` and `.spec.ephemeralContainers` on every pod and flag any container with `securityContext.privileged: true`, with `securityContext.procMount: Unmasked`, or with `securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation` absent or true. Write the absent test as an explicit null comparison: jq's `//` operator treats `false` as empty, so the shorthand `(.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation // true) == true` selects the compliant containers as well and turns the whole query into noise. Second, dump every workload controller (Deployment, DaemonSet, StatefulSet, ReplicaSet, ReplicationController, Job, CronJob) and apply the same test to `.spec.template.spec` — and to `.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec` for CronJobs, whose pod template sits one level deeper. A multi-type `get` populates `kind` on each item, which is what lets one query attribute a finding to the right object. For each hit record the owning controller from `.metadata.ownerReferences` so the finding names an object an engineer can actually edit, and collapse ReplicaSet hits into their owning Deployment rather than reporting both.
api: jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []) + ($p.spec.ephemeralContainers // []))[] | select(.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation == null or .securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation == true) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, .name, (if .securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation == null then "unset" else (.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation|tostring) end)] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $w | (if $w.spec.jobTemplate then $w.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec else $w.spec.template.spec end) as $s | select($s != null) | ($s.containers + ($s.initContainers // []))[] | select(.securityContext.privileged == true or .securityContext.procMount == "Unmasked" or .securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation == null or .securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation == true) | [$w.kind, $w.metadata.namespace, $w.metadata.name, .name, (if .securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation == null then "unset" else (.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation|tostring) end)] | @tsv' collect/controllers.json
controls.evidence: Per offending container: the namespace, pod name, container name, the container list it came from (containers, initContainers or ephemeralContainers) and the verbatim `securityContext` object from `collect/pods.json`, together with the owning controller kind and name from `.metadata.ownerReferences`; for template-level findings, the controller kind, namespace, name and the `securityContext` block from its pod template in `collect/controllers.json`. For `allowPrivilegeEscalation` findings the evidence must state whether the key was absent or explicitly true, since the two are remediated the same way but read differently in a diff.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when no container, init container or ephemeral container in any namespace — in a live pod or in any workload controller's pod template — sets `securityContext.privileged: true` or `securityContext.procMount: Unmasked`, and every one of them carries `securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation` present and equal to false. An absent `allowPrivilegeEscalation` key is FAIL, not PASS. Privileged infrastructure agents may be recorded as accepted exceptions only where each is named individually by namespace, controller kind and container name with a written justification; a blanket namespace exclusion does not satisfy the rule. Where `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces` is refused for lack of cluster-wide list permission, the verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, never PASS on the namespaces that were readable.
controls.remediation: Remove `privileged: true` and set `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` in each container's `securityContext`, then re-roll the controller so the running pods are replaced. Where a container needs one specific kernel privilege, replace the privileged flag with the single capability that grants it (see 2.7) rather than the whole set. Prevent regression at admission by enforcing the `restricted` Pod Security Standard on the namespace (2.1), which rejects both settings, or by a Kyverno/Gatekeeper policy in enforcing mode where a webhook is already the enforcement point.
controls.caveat: Four false passes sit in this control. First, inherited-versus-set: `allowPrivilegeEscalation` defaults to true when the key is absent, so the overwhelmingly common state — no `securityContext` at all — is non-compliant while reading as 'nothing flagged' to a check that looks for the literal value true. Second, the jq idiom for that test is itself a trap in the opposite direction: `//` returns its right-hand side for `false` as well as `null`, so `(.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation // true) == true` reports every compliant container as a violation and, once an assessor dismisses the query as broken and drops it, leaves the control unchecked; compare against null explicitly. Third, neither `privileged` nor `allowPrivilegeEscalation` exists in the pod-level `.spec.securityContext` — they are container-level fields only, so an assessor who reads `.spec.securityContext` finds nothing anywhere in the cluster and reports it clean. Fourth, live pods and controller templates are different populations: a pods-only sweep misses a CronJob that has not fired and a Deployment scaled to zero, while a controllers-only sweep misses bare pods, operator-created pods and static pods, so both dumps are required. Note also that `privileged: true` is not the only route to the same power: CAP_SYS_ADMIN (2.7), a hostPath mount of the container runtime socket (2.4) and hostPID (2.3) are each equivalent, so a PASS here is not a statement about privilege as a whole.

controls.title: Pods stay out of the node's process, IPC and network namespaces
controls.objective: Sharing a host namespace removes the isolation that makes a container a security boundary. hostPID exposes every process on the node — including their command lines and /proc/<pid>/root, which is a path into other containers' filesystems. hostIPC exposes shared memory belonging to other workloads. hostNetwork gives the pod the node's network identity, reachability to node-local services such as the kubelet port and the cloud instance metadata endpoint, and immunity from NetworkPolicy.
controls.procedure: Using the same cluster-wide `collect/pods.json` and `collect/controllers.json` dumps as 2.2 (both taken with `--all-namespaces`, since Pods and every controller kind are namespaced), test `.spec.hostPID`, `.spec.hostIPC` and `.spec.hostNetwork` on each pod and on each controller's pod template, branching explicitly on `.spec.jobTemplate` for CronJobs. These three are pod-level fields, unlike the container-level fields in 2.2, and all three default to false, so an absent key is genuinely compliant. Do not confuse `.spec.shareProcessNamespace`, which shares the PID namespace between containers of the same pod and is not a host-namespace escape. Separately enumerate every container port that declares `hostPort` — across `.spec.containers` and `.spec.initContainers` — because a hostPort binds a listener on the node's address and opens node-level exposure without the pod ever setting hostNetwork. Cross-reference each hostNetwork pod against the NetworkPolicy inventory used in 2.13 and against `.spec.nodeName`, so the report states which nodes carry pods that are outside network policy entirely.
api: jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.hostPID == true or .spec.hostIPC == true or .spec.hostNetwork == true) | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, ((.spec.hostPID // false)|tostring), ((.spec.hostIPC // false)|tostring), ((.spec.hostNetwork // false)|tostring), (.spec.nodeName // "unscheduled")] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] as $c | $c.ports[]? | select(.hostPort != null) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, (.hostPort|tostring), (.containerPort|tostring)] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $w | (if $w.spec.jobTemplate then $w.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec else $w.spec.template.spec end) as $s | select($s != null) | select($s.hostPID == true or $s.hostIPC == true or $s.hostNetwork == true) | [$w.kind, $w.metadata.namespace, $w.metadata.name, (("hostPID=" + (($s.hostPID // false)|tostring))), (("hostIPC=" + (($s.hostIPC // false)|tostring))), (("hostNetwork=" + (($s.hostNetwork // false)|tostring)))] | @tsv' collect/controllers.json

jq -r '.items[] as $w | (if $w.spec.jobTemplate then $w.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec else $w.spec.template.spec end) as $s | select($s != null) | ($s.containers + ($s.initContainers // []))[] as $c | $c.ports[]? | select(.hostPort != null) | [$w.kind, $w.metadata.namespace, $w.metadata.name, $c.name, (.hostPort|tostring)] | @tsv' collect/controllers.json
controls.evidence: Per offending pod: namespace, pod name, the boolean value of each of `hostPID`, `hostIPC` and `hostNetwork` as read from `collect/pods.json`, and the node name from `.spec.nodeName`; per hostPort finding, the namespace, pod, container name, container port and host port number; and for controller-template findings the controller kind, namespace, name and which of the three fields is set, from `collect/controllers.json`. The evidence must also carry the list of hostNetwork pods paired with their nodes, since that list is what qualifies the NetworkPolicy coverage claimed in 2.13.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when no pod and no workload-controller pod template in any namespace sets `hostPID: true`, `hostIPC: true` or `hostNetwork: true`, and no container or init container in either population declares a `hostPort`. Cluster infrastructure that legitimately requires host networking — a CNI agent, kube-proxy, an ingress controller bound to node ports — may be listed as a named exception identified by namespace, controller kind and name, with a justification and a stated compensating control that does not rely on NetworkPolicy; the count of such exceptions is part of the evidence, and an unenumerated exclusion of kube-system is not acceptable. Where the cluster-wide pod list is refused for lack of permission, the verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW.
controls.remediation: Delete the `hostPID`, `hostIPC` and `hostNetwork` keys from the pod spec and let them default to false. Replace hostPort exposure with a Service of type NodePort or LoadBalancer, or with an ingress controller, so the exposure is a reviewable API object rather than a node-local bind. Where host networking is unavoidable, pin the workload to a dedicated node pool, and enforce the `baseline` Pod Security Standard on all other namespaces (2.1), which rejects all three fields and constrains hostPort.
controls.caveat: The important trap is downstream, not in the query: a pod with `hostNetwork: true` is not subject to NetworkPolicy at all, because policy is enforced on the pod network and this pod is on the node's. A clean 2.13 verdict therefore says nothing about these pods, and reporting default-deny coverage without excluding them overstates isolation. A hostPort achieves node-level exposure without hostNetwork and is likewise unmediated by policy on most CNIs, so a query that tests only the three boolean fields under-reports — and testing only `.spec.containers` for ports misses an init container that binds one. hostNetwork also grants unmediated reach to the cloud instance metadata service, which on a node with an over-permissive instance profile is a direct credential-theft path, so assess it together with the node's IAM role rather than on its own. Unlike 2.2's `allowPrivilegeEscalation`, all three fields here default to false, so an absent key really is compliant; carrying the inherited-versus-set rule across from that control generates false findings on every pod in the cluster. Finally do not read `.spec.shareProcessNamespace` as a host-namespace flag — it shares PIDs between containers of one pod and is a different risk.

controls.title: No workload mounts a node filesystem path, and none mounts the container runtime socket
controls.objective: A hostPath volume places a directory from the node inside the container. Mounting the container runtime socket (containerd, CRI-O or Docker) is an immediate, complete node takeover: the pod can start a privileged container of its choosing. Mounting the kubelet directory yields every service-account token on the node. Even a read-only mount of a node directory discloses node state and, via /var/log, has been the pivot for well-known container escapes. Workload pods should reach persistent storage through a PersistentVolumeClaim backed by network or cloud storage, never through the node filesystem.
controls.procedure: From the cluster-wide pod and controller dumps, extract every entry of `.spec.volumes` that carries a `hostPath` key, recording the path and the `hostPath.type`. Classify each path against a high-risk list evaluated explicitly rather than by eyeball: `/var/run/docker.sock`, `/run/docker.sock`, `/run/containerd/containerd.sock`, `/run/crio/crio.sock`, `/var/lib/kubelet`, `/var/lib/docker`, `/var/lib/containerd`, `/etc/kubernetes`, `/etc`, `/root`, `/home`, `/proc`, `/sys`, `/dev`, `/var/log` and bare `/`. Then join the volume to the container `volumeMounts` that consume it — across `.spec.containers` and `.spec.initContainers` — since `readOnly` is a property of the mount and not of the volume, and record `mountPropagation`, because `Bidirectional` lets the container mount into the node. Do not stop at hostPath: resolve every `.spec.volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim` to its bound PersistentVolume and check for `.spec.local.path` or a legacy `.spec.hostPath`, because a local PV is a node directory wearing a PVC. PersistentVolumes are cluster-scoped so one listing covers them, but the PersistentVolumeClaims that bind them are namespaced and must be resolved through `.spec.claimRef` to attribute each PV to a namespace. Finally list CSI inline volumes and their drivers so a driver that projects host paths is reviewed rather than assumed safe.
api: jq -r '.items[] as $w | (if $w.spec.jobTemplate then $w.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec else $w.spec.template.spec end) as $s | select($s != null) | $s.volumes[]? | select(.hostPath != null) | [$w.kind, $w.metadata.namespace, $w.metadata.name, .name, .hostPath.path, (.hostPath.type // "unset")] | @tsv' collect/controllers.json

kubectl --context <ctx> get persistentvolumes -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.local != null or .spec.hostPath != null) | [.metadata.name, ((.spec.local.path) // (.spec.hostPath.path)), (.spec.claimRef.namespace // "-"), (.spec.claimRef.name // "-"), (.status.phase // "-")] | @tsv'
jq -r '.items[] as $p | $p.spec.volumes[]? | select(.csi != null) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, .name, .csi.driver, ((.csi.readOnly // false)|tostring)] | @tsv' collect/pods.json
controls.evidence: For each finding: namespace, pod (or controller kind and name), volume name, the exact `hostPath.path` and `hostPath.type` values, the container and `mountPath` that consume it, and the `readOnly` and `mountPropagation` values from the volumeMount — all quoted from `collect/pods.json` or `collect/controllers.json`. For PVC-routed findings, the PersistentVolume name, its `.spec.local.path` or `.spec.hostPath.path`, its phase, and the `claimRef` namespace and name that tie it to the workload, together with the pod volume entry naming that claim. For CSI inline volumes, the driver name, since the risk verdict depends on what that driver projects.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when no pod and no controller pod template declares a `hostPath` volume, no PersistentVolume of `local` or `hostPath` type is bound to a claim used by any workload namespace, no container or init container declares `mountPropagation: Bidirectional`, and every CSI inline driver in use appears on a reviewed allowlist. Any mount whose path resolves to a container runtime socket, to `/var/lib/kubelet`, or to `/` is FAIL regardless of `readOnly`. Node-agent DaemonSets (CNI, CSI node plugin, log shipper, node exporter) may be recorded as named exceptions with their exact paths listed; the exception is granted per workload and per path, never per namespace. Where the cluster-wide pod list or the PersistentVolume list is refused for lack of permission, the verdict is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW.
controls.remediation: Replace the hostPath with an `emptyDir` where the data is scratch, or with a PersistentVolumeClaim against a network or cloud-backed StorageClass where it is not. For log or metric collection, consume the Kubernetes API or a sidecar rather than reading node directories. Where a node agent must read a host path, restrict it to the narrowest directory, set `readOnly: true` on every mount, set `hostPath.type` to the precise expected type (`File`, `Socket`, `Directory`) so a missing path fails loudly instead of being created, and keep the agent in its own namespace with its own ServiceAccount. Enforce the `baseline` Pod Security Standard (2.1), which rejects hostPath volumes outright.
controls.caveat: The largest gap is the PVC path: a pod whose volume list contains no `hostPath` key can still be mounting a node directory through a PersistentVolumeClaim bound to a `local` PersistentVolume, so a hostPath-only query returns a clean estate while the same directory is mounted — and because PersistentVolumes are cluster-scoped while the claims are namespaced, the attribution only works by resolving `.spec.claimRef`. `readOnly: true` is mitigation, not compliance: a read-only mount of `/var/log` is the documented path to reading arbitrary node files through symlink resolution, and a read-only mount of `/` still discloses node configuration and other pods' storage. An unset `hostPath.type` means the kubelet creates the path if it does not exist, so an apparently harmless mount can bring a new directory into being on every node in the cluster. The volume and the mount are separate objects — the volume list says what is available and the container's `volumeMounts` says what is actually mapped and whether it is writable — so a volume-only check cannot state impact, and a mounts query that reads only `.spec.containers` misses an init container that writes to the path before the app container mounts it read-only. Finally a CSI inline volume is not evidence of safety: the risk depends entirely on what the named driver projects, so an unrecognised driver is a review item and not a pass.

controls.title: Containers execute under a non-root UID that admission can verify before the pod starts
controls.objective: A container process running as UID 0 shares the node kernel with root privileges inside its namespace; combined with any capability, writable mount or kernel vulnerability it converts a container compromise into a node compromise. Every container should declare a non-zero `runAsUser` and set `runAsNonRoot: true`, so that the requirement is expressed in the API and enforceable at admission rather than left to the image's USER directive.
controls.procedure: Collect the pod and controller inventories cluster-wide with `--all-namespaces` before any analysis; pods and every workload controller are namespaced objects, so a dump taken without that flag covers only the namespace bound to the current context and every subsequent query reports a clean result from one namespace of evidence. Then, for every container, init container and ephemeral container, compute the effective security context rather than reading one level: the container's own `securityContext.runAsUser` and `runAsNonRoot` take precedence field by field, and only where a field is absent does the pod-level `.spec.securityContext` apply. Absence is the test, not falsiness — resolve the inheritance with an explicit null-check, because a `//`-style default treats an explicit `runAsNonRoot: false` on the container as if the field were missing and silently substitutes the pod's `true`. Flag any container whose effective `runAsNonRoot` is not literally true, and any whose effective `runAsUser` is 0 or unset. Init containers count: one running as root can write into a shared volume that the main container then executes. Cross-check the runtime outcome by listing pods whose container statuses show `CreateContainerConfigError`, which is how the kubelet reports a `runAsNonRoot: true` container whose image's USER resolves to root; those pods prove the setting was present but the image was never compliant. Finally record any pod with `.spec.hostUsers: false`, because user-namespace remapping changes what UID 0 means and must be stated rather than silently scored.
api: jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] as $c | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, (if $c.securityContext.runAsNonRoot != null then ($c.securityContext.runAsNonRoot|tostring) + " (container)" elif $p.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot != null then ($p.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot|tostring) + " (pod)" else "unset" end), (if $c.securityContext.runAsUser != null then ($c.securityContext.runAsUser|tostring) + " (container)" elif $p.spec.securityContext.runAsUser != null then ($p.spec.securityContext.runAsUser|tostring) + " (pod)" else "unset" end), (if $c.securityContext.runAsGroup != null then ($c.securityContext.runAsGroup|tostring) + " (container)" elif $p.spec.securityContext.runAsGroup != null then ($p.spec.securityContext.runAsGroup|tostring) + " (pod)" else "unset" end)] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []) + ($p.spec.ephemeralContainers // []))[] as $c | (if $c.securityContext.runAsNonRoot != null then $c.securityContext.runAsNonRoot elif $p.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot != null then $p.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot else null end) as $nr | (if $c.securityContext.runAsUser != null then $c.securityContext.runAsUser elif $p.spec.securityContext.runAsUser != null then $p.spec.securityContext.runAsUser else null end) as $uid | select($nr != true or $uid == null or $uid == 0) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, ($nr|tostring), ($uid|tostring), ($p.status.phase // "-")] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $w | (($w.spec.template.spec) // ($w.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec)) as $s | select($s != null) | ($s.containers + ($s.initContainers // []))[] as $c | (if $c.securityContext.runAsNonRoot != null then $c.securityContext.runAsNonRoot elif $s.securityContext.runAsNonRoot != null then $s.securityContext.runAsNonRoot else null end) as $nr | (if $c.securityContext.runAsUser != null then $c.securityContext.runAsUser elif $s.securityContext.runAsUser != null then $s.securityContext.runAsUser else null end) as $uid | select($nr != true or $uid == null or $uid == 0) | [$w.kind, $w.metadata.namespace, $w.metadata.name, $c.name, ($nr|tostring), ($uid|tostring)] | @tsv' collect/controllers.json
controls.evidence: A per-container table from `collect/pods.json` giving namespace, pod, container, the effective `runAsNonRoot` and `runAsUser` values and which level (container or pod) supplied each, with `unset` recorded distinctly from an explicit `false`; the same table for controller pod templates from `collect/controllers.json`, naming the controller kind; and for any runtime failure, the verbatim `.status.containerStatuses[].state.waiting.message` text showing the kubelet's refusal to start a root image. Record the exact collection commands so the reader can see the inventory was cluster-wide.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, for every container, init container and ephemeral container in every namespace — in live pods and in every workload-controller pod template — the effective `runAsNonRoot` (container value if the field is present, otherwise the pod value) is literally `true` and the effective `runAsUser` is an integer greater than 0, and no container status carries `CreateContainerConfigError` with a waiting message naming `runAsNonRoot` (that same reason raised by a missing ConfigMap or Secret is a different defect and does not decide this control). A container whose effective `runAsNonRoot` is true but whose effective `runAsUser` is unset counts as a pass only where the pod's `.status.phase` is `Running`, since the kubelet has then actually admitted the image; the same container in a workload with zero replicas, in a CronJob that has not yet fired, or in a pod that is `Pending` is a fail. Any query in this control run against an inventory not collected with `--all-namespaces` makes the result inconclusive rather than a pass.
controls.remediation: Set `securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: <uid>, runAsGroup: <gid> }` on each container, and give the image a matching `USER` directive so it works outside Kubernetes too. For images that insist on binding a low port as root, use `capabilities.add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]` on a non-root UID instead of running as root, or move the listener above port 1024 and let the Service map it. Where the filesystem needs group ownership, set `fsGroup` at pod level. Enforce the `restricted` Pod Security Standard on the namespace (2.1), which requires `runAsNonRoot` at admission, so that a future manifest cannot reintroduce root.
controls.caveat: Inherited-versus-set is the whole difficulty here, and it produces two opposite reporting errors. The container-level `securityContext` overrides the pod level field by field, so a pod that reads as compliant at `.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` can contain one container with `runAsUser: 0` that runs as root — a pod-level-only check systematically under-reports. The inverse error is in the resolution itself: an alternative-operator default such as `.securityContext.runAsNonRoot // .spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot` cannot distinguish an absent field from an explicit `false`, because both are falsy, so a container that deliberately sets `runAsNonRoot: false` inherits the pod's `true` and is printed as compliant — the inheritance must be resolved with a null test. The second false pass: `runAsNonRoot: true` with no `runAsUser` does not choose a UID, it only asks the kubelet to refuse the container if the image's USER resolves to 0, and that refusal happens at container start. A workload scaled to zero, a CronJob that has never fired or a Deployment whose pods are Pending therefore looks compliant in the API while its image would run as root the moment it starts. Third, a numeric `runAsUser` can be defeated by a later image change unless `runAsNonRoot: true` is present too, so the two fields are a pair, not alternatives. Fourth, pods and controllers are namespaced: a `kubectl get pods` without `--all-namespaces` reads only the context's namespace and returns a clean result that means nothing. Finally, if the cluster runs pods with `hostUsers: false`, UID 0 inside the pod maps to an unprivileged UID on the node and the risk is materially lower — record that fact rather than scoring the pod as if it were host root.

controls.title: Container root filesystems are immutable, with writable paths declared as explicit volumes
controls.objective: A read-only root filesystem removes the attacker's simplest post-exploitation step: dropping a tool, a webshell or a modified binary into the container and persisting across a process restart. It also makes the workload's writable surface explicit — every path that genuinely needs to be written becomes a declared volume that a reviewer can see, rather than an unbounded container layer.
controls.procedure: Working from pod and controller inventories collected with `--all-namespaces`, read `securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem` on every container and init container and flag anything that is not explicitly `true`. This is a container-level field with no pod-level equivalent, so there is no inheritance to resolve — but its absence means writable, which is the state to flag. Then, for each container that does set it, enumerate every volumeMount that is not `readOnly: true`, not only the `emptyDir` ones, and resolve each mount back to the volume source that supplies it (`emptyDir`, `hostPath`, `persistentVolumeClaim`, `csi`) so the report says what kind of writable storage was reopened. Judge whether the mount reinstates something material: a writable `/tmp` or `/var/run` is normal, whereas a writable `/etc`, `/usr`, `/opt` or the container's own `workingDir` reinstates exactly the persistence the control was meant to remove. Record `subPath` where present, since a subPath mount can place a writable file inside an otherwise untouched directory. Where the engagement permits an interactive check on a non-production workload, attempt a write to `/` through `kubectl exec` as direct proof rather than inferring from the manifest.
api: jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] as $c | select(($c.securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem // false) != true) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $w | (($w.spec.template.spec) // ($w.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec)) as $s | select($s != null) | ($s.containers + ($s.initContainers // []))[] as $c | select(($c.securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem // false) != true) | [$w.kind, $w.metadata.namespace, $w.metadata.name, $c.name] | @tsv' collect/controllers.json

jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.volumes // []) as $vols | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] as $c | (($c.volumeMounts // [])[] | select(.readOnly != true)) as $m | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, $m.name, $m.mountPath, ($m.subPath // "-"), (first($vols[] | select(.name == $m.name) | ((keys_unsorted - ["name"])[0])) // "unknown")] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] as $c | (($c.volumeMounts // [])[] | select(.readOnly != true)) as $m | select(($m.mountPath | test("^/(etc|usr|bin|sbin|lib|lib64|opt|boot|root|srv)(/|$)")) or ($m.mountPath == ($c.workingDir // " "))) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, $m.mountPath, ($c.workingDir // "-")] | @tsv' collect/pods.json
controls.evidence: Per container: namespace, pod (or controller kind and name), container name and the literal value or the absence of `securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem`, quoted from the collected JSON; plus, for every container, the full list of writable volumeMounts with volume name, `mountPath`, `subPath` and the resolved volume source kind, so the report states what remains writable, where, and on what medium. Any interactive write attempt is recorded with the exact command and its complete output, including the error text when the write was refused.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every container and init container in every namespace sets `securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` in both live pods and controller pod templates, and no volumeMount lacking `readOnly: true` has a `mountPath` that is equal to or nested under `/etc`, `/usr`, `/bin`, `/sbin`, `/lib`, `/lib64`, `/opt`, `/boot`, `/root` or `/srv`, or is equal to that container's declared `workingDir`. Writable mounts on scratch paths such as `/tmp`, `/var/run` and a dedicated cache directory do not affect the verdict provided each is enumerated in the evidence with its volume source kind.
controls.remediation: Set `securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` on every container and add an `emptyDir` volume for each path the process genuinely writes — typically `/tmp`, a PID or socket directory, and any cache. Where a framework insists on writing into its installation directory, fix it at build time by relocating the writable path through configuration or an environment variable rather than by reverting the setting. Use `emptyDir.medium: Memory` with a `sizeLimit` for scratch that should never touch the node disk, and mark every mount that only needs reading as `readOnly: true`. Enforce the requirement through a Kyverno or Gatekeeper policy in enforcing mode, since the `restricted` Pod Security Standard does not itself require this field.
controls.caveat: Three ways to score this wrongly. First, absence of the key means the root filesystem is writable — the default is false — so a container with no `securityContext` at all is a finding, and a check that searches for the literal value `false` finds nothing and reports a clean cluster. Second, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` describes only the container's own image layer; a volume mounted over any path is writable regardless, so a container that sets the flag and then mounts storage at `/etc` or over its own code directory has no immutability where it counts. The flag alone is therefore not the control — the volumeMount list has to be read alongside it and the finding must name the paths that remain writable. Third, and this is the false pass that survives a careful-looking check, enumerating only `emptyDir` volumes misses the writable mounts that matter most: a `hostPath`, a PersistentVolumeClaim or a CSI volume mounted read-write over a system directory is invisible to an emptyDir-only query, so the inventory must start from every volumeMount that is not `readOnly: true` and resolve its source afterwards. Note also that this is a level 2 control precisely because many stock images write into their root filesystem at start-up, so a wholesale rollout without the accompanying volumes will crash-loop workloads; stage it and verify pod readiness after each change.

controls.title: Containers drop every Linux capability and add back only the ones named and justified
controls.objective: A container that is not privileged still receives a default set of capabilities from the container runtime, several of which are directly attackable — NET_RAW permits ARP and DNS spoofing against every other pod on the network, and DAC_OVERRIDE, SETUID and SETGID undermine in-container privilege separation. The secure state is an explicit `drop: ["ALL"]` on every container, with any required capability added back by name so it is visible in review.
controls.procedure: For every container and init container in the cluster-wide pod inventory and in every controller pod template, read `securityContext.capabilities.drop` and `securityContext.capabilities.add`; capabilities is a container-level field with no pod-level equivalent, so there is no inheritance to resolve. Flag any container whose drop list does not contain the exact uppercase string `ALL`, and separately flag every capability present in an add list, normalising each entry to upper case and stripping any `CAP_` prefix before matching so that a lower-case or prefixed spelling is not missed. Classify the node-escape-adjacent additions — SYS_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, SYS_MODULE, SYS_BOOT, SYS_RAWIO, DAC_READ_SEARCH, BPF, PERFMON, NET_ADMIN, NET_RAW and a literal `ALL` — apart from the benign ones such as NET_BIND_SERVICE and CHOWN. Because the intersection of drop-ALL and a later add is what actually lands, compute the effective set per container rather than reporting the two lists separately, and list separately every container with `privileged: true`, whose capability block is decorative because the runtime grants the full set anyway. Where an interactive check is permitted, confirm the effective set at runtime by reading the CapPrm, CapEff and CapBnd bitmasks from `/proc/1/status` inside the container and decoding them with `capsh --decode=<mask>`; that is the only evidence that reflects the runtime's default set rather than the manifest's silence about it.
api: jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] as $c | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, (($c.securityContext.capabilities.drop // []) | join(",")), (($c.securityContext.capabilities.add // []) | join(","))] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] as $c | select((($c.securityContext.capabilities.drop // []) | index("ALL")) == null) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, (($c.securityContext.capabilities.drop // []) | join(","))] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] as $c | (($c.securityContext.capabilities.add // []) | map(ascii_upcase | ltrimstr("CAP_"))) as $add | select($add | any(. == "SYS_ADMIN" or . == "SYS_PTRACE" or . == "SYS_MODULE" or . == "SYS_BOOT" or . == "SYS_RAWIO" or . == "DAC_READ_SEARCH" or . == "BPF" or . == "PERFMON" or . == "NET_ADMIN" or . == "NET_RAW" or . == "ALL")) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, ($add | join(","))] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] as $c | select($c.securityContext.privileged == true) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, (($c.securityContext.capabilities.drop // []) | join(","))] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $w | (($w.spec.template.spec) // ($w.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec)) as $s | select($s != null) | ($s.containers + ($s.initContainers // []))[] as $c | select((($c.securityContext.capabilities.drop // []) | index("ALL")) == null) | [$w.kind, $w.metadata.namespace, $w.metadata.name, $c.name, (($c.securityContext.capabilities.drop // []) | join(","))] | @tsv' collect/controllers.json
controls.evidence: Per container: namespace, pod (or controller kind and name), container name, the verbatim `capabilities.drop` and `capabilities.add` arrays from the collected JSON, and the derived effective capability set, with the normalisation applied to each add entry shown. Containers with `privileged: true` are listed separately alongside their drop list, to show that the drop has no effect there. Where runtime confirmation was taken, the raw `CapPrm`/`CapEff`/`CapBnd` hex values from `/proc/1/status` together with the `capsh --decode` output naming each capability actually held.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every container and init container in every namespace, in live pods and in controller pod templates, sets `securityContext.capabilities.drop` containing the literal uppercase entry `ALL`, no container sets `securityContext.privileged: true`, and every entry in any `capabilities.add` list — compared upper-cased and with a `CAP_` prefix stripped — is a member of the engagement's recorded allowlist, which by default contains only `NET_BIND_SERVICE`. Any add of `ALL`, SYS_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, SYS_MODULE, SYS_BOOT, SYS_RAWIO, DAC_READ_SEARCH, BPF, PERFMON, NET_ADMIN or NET_RAW is a fail unless it appears in that allowlist against a named infrastructure component.
controls.remediation: Set `securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` on every container and add back only what the process demonstrably needs, verified by running it and reading the failure rather than by guessing. Spell the drop entry in upper case, since the value is matched literally. Replace SYS_ADMIN — which is close to full privilege — with the specific narrower capability, or restructure the workload so the privileged step happens outside the cluster. Enforce the `restricted` Pod Security Standard on the namespace (2.1), which requires `drop: ["ALL"]` and permits only `NET_BIND_SERVICE` to be added back.
controls.caveat: This is the archetypal false-pass control. The container runtime grants a default capability set — CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FOWNER, FSETID, KILL, SETGID, SETUID, SETPCAP, NET_BIND_SERVICE, NET_RAW, SYS_CHROOT, MKNOD and AUDIT_WRITE — to every container that says nothing, so a container with an empty or absent `add` list is not capability-free, and a check that only looks for dangerous additions reports a clean cluster that is running NET_RAW everywhere. Only an explicit `drop: ["ALL"]` removes them. That value is matched case-sensitively, so `drop: ["all"]` is not recognised as the wildcard and drops nothing while reading as a compliant manifest; conversely an `add` list is easy to under-match, because `cap_net_admin` and `NET_ADMIN` are the same grant written two ways and only the normalised comparison catches both. A drop of ALL followed by `add: ["ALL"]` restores the entire set and must be treated as the worst case, not as a compliant drop. `privileged: true` (2.2) grants the full set regardless of any drop list, so a privileged container cannot pass this control whatever its capabilities block says; settle 2.2 first and report the two together. Manifest evidence describes intent, not the running kernel state: only the `/proc/1/status` masks show what the process actually holds, which matters when a mutating webhook or a policy engine has rewritten the spec after submission.

controls.title: Pods that never call the API get no service-account token mounted
controls.objective: By default every pod receives a projected service-account token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount, so any code execution in any container yields a cluster credential the attacker can immediately replay against the API server. A workload that does not talk to the Kubernetes API should have no token mounted at all, which removes that step entirely rather than relying on the token's permissions being small.
controls.procedure: The effective mount decision has three inputs and all three must be resolved: the pod's `.spec.automountServiceAccountToken` wins if the field is present; otherwise the ServiceAccount named by `.spec.serviceAccountName` (defaulting to `default`, in the pod's own namespace) supplies its own `automountServiceAccountToken`; and if the field is absent from both, the token is mounted. Collect ServiceAccounts with `--all-namespaces` and pods cluster-wide, record for each object whether the field is true, false or absent — testing presence, not truthiness, so that an explicit `false` is never confused with an unset field — then join the two by namespace and ServiceAccount name to compute the effective outcome per pod together with the level that decided it. Then check what actually appears in the container: enumerate projected volumes whose sources include a `serviceAccountToken`, which mount a token regardless of the automount flag, recording the audience and `expirationSeconds` of each, and enumerate every volumeMount whose path is under the service-account directory, attributing it to the container that mounts it. Separately list long-lived Secrets of type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token`, which since v1.24 are only created deliberately and hold non-expiring credentials.
api: jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, (if has("automountServiceAccountToken") then (.automountServiceAccountToken|tostring) else "unset" end), ((.secrets // []) | length | tostring)] | @tsv' collect/serviceaccounts.json

jq -r --slurpfile sa collect/serviceaccounts.json '($sa[0].items | map({key: (.metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name), value: (if has("automountServiceAccountToken") then .automountServiceAccountToken else null end)}) | from_entries) as $samap | .items[] | (.spec.serviceAccountName // "default") as $san | (if .spec.automountServiceAccountToken != null then {v: .spec.automountServiceAccountToken, src: "pod"} elif ($samap[.metadata.namespace + "/" + $san] != null) then {v: $samap[.metadata.namespace + "/" + $san], src: "serviceaccount"} else {v: true, src: "cluster-default(mounted)"} end) as $eff | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, $san, ($eff.v|tostring), $eff.src] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.volumes // [])[] | select((.projected.sources // []) | any(.serviceAccountToken != null)) | . as $v | ($v.projected.sources[] | select(.serviceAccountToken != null) | .serviceAccountToken) as $t | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $v.name, ($t.audience // "kubernetes-default"), (($t.expirationSeconds // "cluster-default")|tostring)] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

kubectl --context <ctx> get secrets --all-namespaces --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, (.metadata.annotations["kubernetes.io/service-account.name"] // "-")] | @tsv'
controls.evidence: A joined table keyed by namespace and pod giving the resolved ServiceAccount name, the pod-level and ServiceAccount-level `automountServiceAccountToken` values recorded as true, false or `unset`, the level that decided the outcome, and the computed effective result; plus, for any pod with a projected token volume, the volume name, audience and `expirationSeconds`, and the container that mounts it; plus the list of long-lived `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` Secrets with the ServiceAccount each is annotated to. The `--all-namespaces` collection commands are quoted so the reader can see the inventory was not one namespace.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, for every pod outside the engagement's recorded list of API-calling workloads, the computed effective automount result is false — decided by an explicit `false` on the pod or on its ServiceAccount — and that pod declares no projected volume containing a `serviceAccountToken` source; and when no Secret of type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` exists outside that same recorded list. A pod where the field is absent from both the pod spec and its ServiceAccount is a fail, because the cluster default is to mount. Pods on the recorded list pass this control on the mount question alone; the permissions their ServiceAccount holds are settled by 2.11 and 2.12.
controls.remediation: Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on each ServiceAccount that no workload needs API access through, and set the same field on the pod spec for the case where a shared ServiceAccount serves both API and non-API workloads. For pods that do need API access, give each its own ServiceAccount rather than sharing one, request a short-lived audience-bound token through a projected volume with an explicit `expirationSeconds`, and delete any long-lived `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` Secret in favour of `kubectl create token <sa> --duration=<d>`.
controls.caveat: Inherited-versus-set decides this control and a single-object check gets it wrong in both directions. Reading only ServiceAccounts misses pods that opt back in with `automountServiceAccountToken: true` in the pod spec, which overrides a ServiceAccount that says false; reading only pods misses that an absent pod field falls through to the ServiceAccount, and that absence on both means mounted. The state to flag is therefore absence, not the value true — and because both `false` and absent are falsy, the join must test field presence rather than defaulting one to the other, or a ServiceAccount that explicitly disables the mount becomes indistinguishable from one that never mentioned it. A second bypass: a pod can declare a projected volume with a `serviceAccountToken` source and receive a token whether or not automount is disabled, so the flag alone does not prove no credential is present — the volume list has to be read, and a token with a non-default audience is still a credential for whatever accepts that audience. Third, no token mounted is only harmless if the ServiceAccount is also weak: disabling automount on a ServiceAccount bound to a powerful ClusterRole leaves the escalation path intact for anyone who can create a pod that names it, so this control must be read together with 2.11 and with 2.12 for the `default` ServiceAccount. Finally, ServiceAccounts, pods and Secrets are all namespaced, so a listing without `--all-namespaces` covers exactly one namespace and reads as a clean cluster.

controls.title: No Role or ClusterRole grants a wildcard API group, resource or verb
controls.objective: A wildcard in an RBAC rule grants everything that exists now and everything added later, including custom resources installed after the grant was written. It defeats review, because nobody can state what the holder can do without enumerating the whole API surface, and it silently expands whenever a CRD is installed. Every rule should name its API groups, resources and verbs explicitly.
controls.procedure: ClusterRoles are cluster-scoped and Roles are namespaced, so collect them separately and pass `--all-namespaces` for Roles — a `kubectl get roles` without it reads only the namespace embedded in the selected context and will report a clean cluster from one namespace of evidence. Walk every `.rules[]` entry and flag any that contains `*` in `apiGroups`, `resources` or `verbs`, and separately any that contains `*` in `nonResourceURLs`, which is a different field that a resources-and-verbs check does not see. Record `resourceNames` alongside, because a wildcard verb narrowed to a single named object is materially different from an unrestricted one. Then list every ClusterRole carrying an `aggregationRule` and record both its label selectors and its currently materialised `.rules`, since the controller populates those rules from other ClusterRoles at runtime and the wildcard may arrive later. Finally collect every RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding and join each flagged role to the bindings that reference it, keyed by role kind, scope and name rather than by name alone, so the report separates a live wildcard held by a real subject from a latent one on an unbound role.
api: jq -r '.items[] as $r | $r.rules[]? | select((((.verbs // []) | index("*")) != null) or (((.resources // []) | index("*")) != null) or (((.apiGroups // []) | index("*")) != null)) | [($r.metadata.namespace // "cluster"), $r.metadata.name, ((.apiGroups // []) | join(",")), ((.resources // []) | join(",")), ((.verbs // []) | join(",")), ((.resourceNames // []) | join(","))] | @tsv' collect/clusterroles.json collect/roles.json

jq -r '.items[] as $r | $r.rules[]? | select(((.nonResourceURLs // []) | index("*")) != null) | [$r.metadata.name, ((.nonResourceURLs // []) | join(",")), ((.verbs // []) | join(","))] | @tsv' collect/clusterroles.json
jq -r '.items[] | select(.aggregationRule != null) | [.metadata.name, (.aggregationRule.clusterRoleSelectors | tostring), ((.rules // []) | length | tostring)] | @tsv' collect/clusterroles.json

jq -r --slurpfile b collect/bindings.json '([$b[0].items[] | (.roleRef.kind + "/" + (if .roleRef.kind == "Role" then (.metadata.namespace // "-") else "cluster" end) + "/" + .roleRef.name)] | unique) as $bound | .items[] | select(any(.rules[]?; (((.verbs // []) | index("*")) != null) or (((.resources // []) | index("*")) != null) or (((.apiGroups // []) | index("*")) != null) or (((.nonResourceURLs // []) | index("*")) != null))) | ((if .metadata.namespace then "Role/" + .metadata.namespace else "ClusterRole/cluster" end) + "/" + .metadata.name) as $key | [$key, (if ($bound | index($key)) then "bound" else "latent" end)] | @tsv' collect/clusterroles.json collect/roles.json
controls.evidence: Per finding: the role kind, namespace (or `cluster`), role name, and the verbatim rule object showing which of `apiGroups`, `resources`, `verbs` or `nonResourceURLs` contains the wildcard, quoted from `collect/clusterroles.json` or `collect/roles.json`; the bound-or-latent determination with the RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings whose `roleRef` names that role and their subjects; and for every aggregated ClusterRole, its selectors together with the rule count the controller has currently materialised, so a later expansion is visible as a change.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when no Role in any namespace and no ClusterRole outside the Kubernetes-shipped set whose name begins `system:` — plus the built-in `cluster-admin` — contains `*` in `apiGroups`, `resources`, `verbs` or `nonResourceURLs`, evaluated against the rules as they currently stand, including the rules a controller has materialised into an aggregated ClusterRole. A wildcard in a role that no binding references is reported as latent at reduced severity but still fails the control, because a single binding activates it. The exempted built-in roles are not tested for wildcards here; they are assessed by who is bound to them, under 2.10 and 2.11.
controls.remediation: Rewrite each wildcard rule as an explicit list: name the API group (`""` for core), name each resource including its subresources (`pods`, `pods/log`, `pods/exec` are three distinct entries), and name each verb. Where a role legitimately needs broad read access, bind the built-in `view` ClusterRole rather than authoring a wildcard. Narrow further with `resourceNames` where the subject only ever touches specific objects. After rewriting, confirm no access was lost by comparing `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<subject>` output taken before and after the change.
controls.caveat: Aggregated ClusterRoles are the trap that survives a careful review. A ClusterRole with an `aggregationRule` has its `.rules` written by the controller from every ClusterRole matching its label selectors, so `view` can silently acquire secret-reading power the moment anybody creates a ClusterRole labelled `rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-view: "true"` — you must evaluate the aggregate's materialised rules and its selector, not just the sub-role in front of you, and a wildcard introduced through aggregation appears in an object nobody thought they were editing. `nonResourceURLs` is a separate field from `resources`, so a rule granting `*` on non-resource paths passes a resources-and-verbs check while granting access to `/metrics`, `/debug/pprof` and the rest of the non-resource surface. Roles are namespaced, so the `--all-namespaces` flag is load-bearing rather than stylistic: without it the wildcard in another team's namespace is simply not in the data. Matching bindings to roles by name alone also mis-attributes, because a Role in one namespace and a ClusterRole can share a name and only the kind plus scope distinguishes them. And a wildcard that is not bound to anything is not exploitable today but is one `kubectl create rolebinding` away, so it must not be filtered out of the report as a non-issue.

controls.title: cluster-admin is held by a small, named set of subjects and by no broad group
controls.objective: cluster-admin is unrestricted authority over every object in every namespace, including RBAC itself, so anyone holding it can grant themselves anything and remove the evidence. The set of subjects bound to it should be short, individually named, human-attributable, and free of group subjects that expand membership outside the cluster's own records.
controls.procedure: Collect ClusterRoleBindings, which are cluster-scoped, and RoleBindings with `--all-namespaces`, then expand the `subjects` of every binding whose `roleRef` names `cluster-admin`, recording kind (User, Group, ServiceAccount), namespace for service accounts, and name. Namespaced RoleBindings to the `cluster-admin` ClusterRole matter as much as ClusterRoleBindings: they grant full authority within one namespace, including its Secrets, and are invisible to a ClusterRoleBinding-only query. Next find the roles that are cluster-admin under another name — any ClusterRole with a single rule holding `*` in all three of apiGroups, resources and verbs — and expand the subjects of every binding to those too. Flag every subject of kind Group, and specifically `system:masters`, `system:authenticated`, `system:unauthenticated` and any `system:serviceaccounts` group, since these expand to populations rather than people. Confirm each candidate administrator's effective authority directly with `kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces --as=<subject>`, which answers from the API server's own authorisers and therefore catches admin-equivalence this control's role matching would miss. Finally resolve what each group actually means outside the cluster through the platform's own identity mapping: the `aws-auth` ConfigMap plus EKS access entries and their associated access policies, the project IAM policy for GKE, or the Entra and Azure role assignments for AKS. Without that step the report can name a group but cannot say who is in it.
api: jq -r --slurpfile cr collect/clusterroles.json '((($cr[0].items | map(select(any(.rules[]?; (((.apiGroups // []) | index("*")) != null) and (((.resources // []) | index("*")) != null) and (((.verbs // []) | index("*")) != null)))) | map(.metadata.name)) + ["cluster-admin"]) | unique) as $adminroles | .items[] | select(.roleRef.name as $n | $adminroles | index($n)) | . as $b | ($b.subjects // [])[] | [($b.metadata.namespace // "cluster"), $b.metadata.name, $b.roleRef.name, .kind, (.namespace // "-"), .name] | @tsv' collect/clusterrolebindings.json collect/rolebindings.json

jq -r '.items[] | . as $b | ($b.subjects // [])[] | select(.kind == "Group" and (.name == "system:masters" or .name == "system:authenticated" or .name == "system:unauthenticated" or (.name | startswith("system:serviceaccounts")))) | [($b.metadata.namespace // "cluster"), $b.metadata.name, $b.roleRef.kind, $b.roleRef.name, .name] | @tsv' collect/clusterrolebindings.json collect/rolebindings.json
kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get configmap aws-auth -o yaml
aws eks list-access-entries --cluster-name <cluster> --region <region> && aws eks list-associated-access-policies --cluster-name <cluster> --principal-arn <principal-arn> --region <region>

az aks show -g <rg> -n <cluster> --query '{aad:aadProfile,rbac:enableRbac,localAccounts:disableLocalAccounts}' && az role assignment list --scope /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.ContainerService/managedClusters/<cluster> --include-inherited -o table
controls.evidence: For each binding: the ClusterRoleBinding or RoleBinding name, its namespace or `cluster`, its `roleRef`, and every subject's kind, namespace and name, quoted from `collect/clusterrolebindings.json` and `collect/rolebindings.json`; the names of any ClusterRoles that are wildcard-equivalent to cluster-admin and their bindings; the `kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces --as=<subject>` answer for each candidate administrator; and the platform identity mapping output (aws-auth ConfigMap, EKS access entries with their associated access policies, GCP IAM policy, or AKS aadProfile and Azure role assignments) resolving each Group subject to real principals, or the error returned if that call could not be made.
