A run in which the cloud IAM call failed, was not permitted, or left any Group subject unresolved is inconclusive and must be reported as requiring manual review rather than as a pass.
controls.remediation: Delete unnecessary cluster-admin ClusterRoleBindings and replace each with the narrowest built-in role that covers the actual job — `edit` or `admin` scoped to a namespace through a RoleBinding, or a purpose-written Role. Route human administrator access through a group in the identity provider that is itself audited, and through just-in-time elevation rather than a standing binding. Keep at most one break-glass path, alert on its use from the audit log, and remove any static kubeconfig holding a `system:masters` client certificate, since that credential cannot be revoked through RBAC. On a managed cluster, remove the cloud-side admin grants too — the EKS access policy, the GKE IAM role or the AKS cluster-admin role assignment — because deleting the Kubernetes binding alone leaves them intact.
controls.caveat: RBAC is an upper bound on assurance here, not the whole answer. A client certificate presenting the organisation `system:masters` is authorised by the API server's built-in superuser short-circuit before RBAC is consulted at all; that holder appears in no ClusterRoleBinding and no kubectl query will ever show it, so a clean RBAC result cannot be reported as "only these principals are admin" — state what was checked. On a managed control plane the mapping between cloud identities and Kubernetes subjects lives outside the cluster: an EKS access entry with the cluster-admin access policy or an aws-auth line, a GKE IAM role such as `roles/container.admin`, or an AKS Entra assignment can confer cluster-admin-equivalent power with no RBAC object naming that user, and the cluster-admin credential command on each platform can bypass the identity integration entirely, so the cloud API call is mandatory rather than supplementary and its failure makes the control inconclusive, never a pass. A `roleRef.name == "cluster-admin"` filter also misses any custom ClusterRole holding the triple wildcard, which is the same authority under a different name, and misses namespace-scoped RoleBindings to cluster-admin, which are full control over that namespace including its Secrets. Neither does an admin-role census capture the subject who reaches the same place indirectly — through `escalate`, `bind`, `impersonate`, pod creation with a privileged ServiceAccount, `pods/exec` into a control-plane workload, or cluster-wide secret reads — which is why 2.11 is a separate control and this one cannot be read as "nobody else can take over the cluster".

controls.title: No non-administrative subject holds a permission that is equivalent to cluster takeover
controls.objective: Several ordinary-looking RBAC permissions are cluster-admin by a longer route. Creating a pod lets a subject mount any ServiceAccount in the namespace, or a hostPath, and read the node. Exec or attach on a pod inherits that pod's identity. Reading Secrets cluster-wide harvests every token. Impersonation, `escalate`, `bind`, webhook creation and CSR approval each grant the ability to write the authorisation rules themselves. These must be held only by subjects that are already trusted with the cluster.
controls.procedure: Build the effective permission closure per subject rather than reading roles in isolation. Collect ClusterRoles, all-namespace Roles, ClusterRoleBindings and all-namespace RoleBindings, then join each binding's `roleRef` to its rules and attribute the resulting rule set to each subject, keeping the scope: a ClusterRoleBinding applies everywhere, a RoleBinding to a ClusterRole applies only in its namespace. Match on the (apiGroup, resource, verb) triple, never on the resource name alone, because the verb is what makes a rule dangerous and a CRD may reuse a core resource name. Test for the takeover-equivalent triples explicitly: create/update/patch on `pods` (core), or on any pod-creating controller kind (`deployments`, `daemonsets`, `statefulsets`, `replicasets` in `apps`; `jobs`, `cronjobs` in `batch`); create on `pods/exec`, `pods/attach` or `pods/portforward`; update/patch on `pods/ephemeralcontainers`, which is the verb that subresource actually accepts; get/list/watch on `secrets` without a narrowing `resourceNames`; create on `serviceaccounts/token`; `impersonate` on `users`, `groups` or `serviceaccounts`; `escalate` or `bind` on `roles`/`clusterroles`, and create/update/patch on `rolebindings`/`clusterrolebindings`, in `rbac.authorization.k8s.io`; create/update/patch on validating or mutating webhook configurations; `update` on `certificatesigningrequests/approval` together with `approve` on `signers` in `certificates.k8s.io`, which are the two halves of approving a certificate; and get/create on `nodes/proxy`. Separately list ClusterRoles carrying an `aggregationRule`, whose rule set is written by the aggregation controller and grows whenever a matching labelled ClusterRole is created. Where the assessing credential holds impersonation, corroborate each computed result with `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<subject> --all-namespaces`, which asks the API server's own authoriser and catches paths the join missed.

controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, for every subject outside the client-supplied cluster-administrator set, the computed closure contains none of these triples: create/update/patch on `pods` or on a pod-creating controller kind at cluster scope; create on `pods/exec`, `pods/attach` or `pods/portforward`; update/patch on `pods/ephemeralcontainers`; get/list/watch on `secrets` with an empty `resourceNames`; create on `serviceaccounts/token`; `impersonate`; `escalate` or `bind` on roles or clusterroles, or create/update/patch on rolebindings or clusterrolebindings; create/update/patch on validating or mutating webhook configurations; `update` on `certificatesigningrequests/approval` or `approve` on `signers`; get/create on `nodes/proxy`; or a wildcard (`*`) in apiGroups, resources or verbs that subsumes any of the above. A namespace-scoped grant of pod creation is exempt only where the evidence shows every ServiceAccount in that namespace has an empty cluster-scoped closure. A run that could neither compute the closure from collected rules nor use impersonation is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, never a pass.
controls.remediation: Remove the permission where it is not needed, and where it is, narrow it: scope it to a namespace with a RoleBinding instead of a ClusterRoleBinding, restrict `secrets` access with `resourceNames` naming only the secrets the workload reads, and split read from write. Replace standing `pods/exec` for humans with an audited break-glass procedure. Where an operator needs to create pods, give it its own namespace and ensure no privileged ServiceAccount exists there for it to mount. Enforce pod-level restrictions through Pod Security Admission (2.1) so that even a subject who can create pods cannot create a privileged one, which removes most of the escalation value.
controls.caveat: Four ways this control is scored falsely clean. First, `kubectl auth can-i --as=` requires the `impersonate` verb, which a correctly read-only assessment credential does not hold; the command then returns a 403 that is easy to record as "cannot, therefore compliant". An impersonation failure is inconclusive — fall back to computing the closure from the rules yourself and say which method produced the answer. Second, the dangerous permission is usually indirect: `create` on deployments, daemonsets, statefulsets, jobs, cronjobs or replicasets yields pod creation through the controller with the same effect, and `create` on `serviceaccounts/token` mints a credential for any ServiceAccount in the namespace, so a rule filter written against `resources: ["pods"]` misses the majority of real paths. Third, subresources are distinct resource strings — `pods` does not imply `pods/exec`, and `pods/ephemeralcontainers` accepts update/patch rather than create, so a filter written around `create` misses container injection entirely; matching on the resource alone without the verb is the mirror error and reports every read-only pod viewer as a takeover, which is why the match is on the (apiGroup, resource, verb) triple. Fourth, an aggregated ClusterRole shows only the rules it holds at the moment it is read: its `rules` are written by the aggregation controller from the `aggregationRule` selectors, so a role that reads clean today silently gains new rules the moment anyone creates a ClusterRole carrying a matching label — an aggregated role must be judged on its selectors and on who can create labelled ClusterRoles, not on its current rule set. Note also that `get secrets` narrowed by `resourceNames` is materially weaker than cluster-wide list, so read `resourceNames` before flagging; and that any wildcard found under 2.9 satisfies every item on this list implicitly, so a wildcard finding must be carried into this control rather than counted once.

controls.title: The default ServiceAccount is unused by workloads and carries no permissions
controls.objective: Every namespace gets a `default` ServiceAccount, and every pod that does not name one is silently assigned it. That makes `default` a shared identity across unrelated workloads: any permission granted to it is granted to everything in the namespace, and a compromise of the least important pod yields the same token as the most important. It should have no bindings, no automounted token, and no pods using it.
controls.procedure: Read the live pod objects, not stored manifests, because the API server defaults `.spec.serviceAccountName` at admission and the field is populated on the object even when the author omitted it. List every pod cluster-wide whose resolved ServiceAccount is `default`, and the same for every controller pod template. Then list every `default` ServiceAccount using a field selector across all namespaces and record its `automountServiceAccountToken` value, which sits at the top level of the ServiceAccount object rather than under `spec`. Because that setting is only a default, also record the pod-level `spec.automountServiceAccountToken` — `true` on the pod overrides `false` on the account — and any pod volume that projects a `serviceAccountToken` source directly, which mounts a token irrespective of either setting. Then enumerate every RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding whose subject list contains a ServiceAccount named `default`, and — separately, because a name match will not find them — any binding whose subject is the group `system:serviceaccounts`, `system:serviceaccounts:<namespace>` or `system:authenticated`, each of which confers the grant on every ServiceAccount in scope including default. Where impersonation is available, confirm the resulting authority with `kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:default -n <ns>` for each namespace that has pods on the default account.

kubectl --context <ctx> get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | . as $b | ($b.subjects // [])[] | select((.kind == "ServiceAccount" and .name == "default") or (.kind == "Group" and ((.name | startswith("system:serviceaccounts")) or (.name == "system:authenticated")))) | [($b.metadata.namespace // "cluster-scoped"), $b.metadata.name, $b.roleRef.kind, $b.roleRef.name, .kind, (.namespace // "-"), .name] | @tsv'

controls.verdict_rule: PASS when all of the following hold: no pod and no controller pod template in any namespace resolves to the `default` ServiceAccount; every `default` ServiceAccount sets `automountServiceAccountToken: false`; no pod on the default account sets `spec.automountServiceAccountToken: true` and none declares its own projected `serviceAccountToken` volume (the kubelet-injected `kube-api-access-*` volume does not count); and no RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding grants to a ServiceAccount named `default` or to a `system:serviceaccounts*` group, while any binding to `system:authenticated` resolves only to the built-in discovery roles `system:basic-user`, `system:discovery`, `system:public-info-viewer` and `system:service-account-issuer-discovery`, whose rules are shown to be unmodified. All conditions are required: an unused default that still holds a binding, or a bound-free default that is still mounted into pods, is a fail.
controls.remediation: Create a dedicated ServiceAccount per workload and set `serviceAccountName` explicitly in the pod template, so identity follows the workload rather than the namespace. Patch every default account to stop mounting: `kubectl --context <ctx> -n <ns> patch serviceaccount default -p '{"automountServiceAccountToken":false}'`, and remove any pod-level `automountServiceAccountToken: true` that overrides it. Delete any RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding whose subject is the default ServiceAccount, and replace group-wide `system:serviceaccounts` grants with per-ServiceAccount bindings. Add the per-workload ServiceAccount to the namespace's provisioning template so new workloads are born with their own identity.
controls.caveat: Do not read `serviceAccountName` from a stored or Git manifest: it is empty there and populated by the API server on the live object, so an assessment against source control reports "no pods use default" while every one of them does. The group subject is the second trap — a binding whose subject is `system:serviceaccounts`, `system:serviceaccounts:<ns>` or `system:authenticated` grants to every ServiceAccount in scope without ever naming `default`, so a subject-name match on the string `default` finds nothing and the namespace reads clean while its default account holds real authority; note that every cluster ships benign `system:authenticated` bindings for the discovery roles, so those must be resolved and their rules checked rather than either flagged wholesale or ignored wholesale. Third, `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount is only a default and is overridden by `true` on the pod, and a pod may mount a token regardless by declaring a projected volume with a `serviceAccountToken` source — an assessment that reads only the ServiceAccount field records a token-free namespace whose pods hold tokens, and one that flags every projected token volume mistakes the kubelet's own `kube-api-access-*` injection for an author's choice. Fourth, the two halves are independent: stopping the automount removes the token from pods but leaves the permissions in place for anyone who can create a pod that opts back in (2.11), and removing the bindings leaves a token mounted in every pod that can be replayed if a permission is granted later. Note also that the `default` ServiceAccount cannot be deleted usefully — the controller recreates it — so remediation is patching and unbinding, not removal.

controls.title: Every namespace denies pod traffic by default and the CNI in use actually enforces policy
controls.objective: Without a NetworkPolicy, every pod in the cluster can reach every other pod and every external address, so a single compromised container has flat access to internal services, other tenants' workloads and the cloud metadata endpoint. Each namespace should carry a default-deny policy for both ingress and egress, with explicitly allowed flows added on top — and the cluster's network plugin must be one that implements policy, or the objects are decorative.
controls.procedure: Collect every NetworkPolicy cluster-wide — they are namespaced, so `--all-namespaces` is required or you audit one namespace and report the cluster. A default-deny is a policy that selects every pod in its namespace and denies both directions: `spec.podSelector` must be empty in the sense that it carries no `matchLabels` entries and no `matchExpressions`, since `{}`, `{matchLabels: {}}` and `{matchExpressions: []}` all select every pod but are not equal as JSON; `spec.policyTypes` must list both `Ingress` and `Egress`; and the policy must carry no rules of its own. Compute the set difference between all namespaces and namespaces holding such a policy, so the finding is a list of unprotected namespaces rather than a count. Because policies are additive allow-rules, separately list every rule whose peer list is empty — an ingress entry with no `from`, or an egress entry with no `to` — which re-opens the pods it selects to all sources or all destinations. Then, and this is the part that decides whether the objects mean anything, establish that the network plugin enforces policy: inspect the kube-system DaemonSets, their container images and their environment for Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave or the AWS VPC CNI, read `ENABLE_NETWORK_POLICY` on the `aws-node` DaemonSet where that plugin is in use, list the CRDs the policy-implementing operators install, and on a managed cluster ask the cloud API, since the plugin is a cluster property there rather than something reliably inferable from workloads. Where the engagement allows an active check, run a throwaway pod in one namespace and attempt a connection to a Service ClusterIP in another namespace and to the cloud metadata address; a successful connection under a default-deny policy is direct proof the policy is not enforced.

controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every namespace that hosts workloads contains a NetworkPolicy whose `podSelector` carries no `matchLabels` and no `matchExpressions`, whose `policyTypes` contains both `Ingress` and `Egress`, and which declares no rules; when no other policy in that namespace contains an ingress rule with an empty `from` or an egress rule with an empty `to` selecting the same pods; when the network plugin is identified as one that implements NetworkPolicy and its enforcement is shown enabled by at least one of a Calico, Cilium or Antrea DaemonSet, `ENABLE_NETWORK_POLICY=true` on `aws-node` or the equivalent managed-addon configuration, `networkPolicy.enabled=true` or `datapathProvider=ADVANCED_DATAPATH` on GKE, or a non-empty `networkProfile.networkPolicy` on AKS; and, where an active probe was permitted, the cross-namespace ClusterIP connection attempt fails. A cluster whose plugin does not enforce policy fails regardless of how many policy objects exist; a cluster whose plugin could not be identified is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, not a pass. Pods with `hostNetwork: true` are outside NetworkPolicy entirely and must be listed as excluded rather than counted as covered.
controls.remediation: Apply a default-deny to every namespace: a NetworkPolicy with `spec.podSelector: {}` and `spec.policyTypes: ["Ingress","Egress"]` and no ingress or egress rules. Then add narrow allow policies for the flows the workload genuinely needs, including an egress allow to kube-dns on UDP and TCP 53 which everything requires. Keep the cloud metadata address out of every egress allow by listing `169.254.169.254/32` in the `except` field of each `ipBlock`, since NetworkPolicy has no deny rule and any broad allow otherwise re-opens it. If the current CNI cannot enforce policy, that is the primary remediation — install Calico or Cilium, or enable policy on the existing plugin — and the policies are worthless until it is done.
controls.caveat: The dominant false pass in the whole section: the API server accepts, stores and returns NetworkPolicy objects whether or not anything implements them. Flannel ignores every policy, and the AWS VPC CNI ignores them unless network-policy support is explicitly enabled, so a cluster full of correct default-deny policies can have precisely zero network isolation and will read as fully compliant to an API-only check. Identifying the CNI is therefore part of the control, not context — and on EKS, GKE and AKS the plugin is a cluster property the workload API may not reveal, so the cloud API is the authority and an unidentifiable plugin is inconclusive rather than compliant. Second, an empty selector is not an empty object: `podSelector: {matchLabels: {}}` selects every pod exactly as `{}` does, so a check written as `podSelector == {}` or as a JSON length test on the selector object misses real default-deny policies and reports protected namespaces as unprotected; the mirror-image error, treating any present `podSelector` as selecting everything, reports a policy scoped to one label as cluster-wide protection. Third, `policyTypes` is what makes a policy deny: a policy listing only `Ingress` leaves all egress open, including to the metadata endpoint and to the internet, and an absent `egress` key only denies when `Egress` is in `policyTypes`. Fourth, policies are additive allow-rules, so an ingress rule with an empty `from` or an egress rule with an empty `to` in any other policy re-opens the same pods; the verdict must be computed as the union of policies applying to each pod, not from the presence of one object. Fifth, pods with `hostNetwork: true` (2.3) bypass NetworkPolicy entirely and cannot be counted as covered. Sixth, the active probe fails for the wrong reason if it resolves a DNS name: under a working default-deny, DNS egress is blocked, so `curl http://svc.ns.svc.cluster.local` also fails at resolution on a cluster enforcing nothing — probe a ClusterIP or pod IP directly, and treat a resolution error as an inconclusive probe rather than proof of isolation. Finally, NetworkPolicy objects are namespaced, so a listing without `--all-namespaces` audits the context's default namespace and reports the cluster on that basis.

controls.title: Secret material is encrypted at rest under a managed key, and application credentials are sourced from an external store
controls.objective: A Kubernetes Secret is base64-encoded, not encrypted: anyone who can read the object, or read etcd, holds the plaintext. The cluster should encrypt Secrets at rest with a key held in a KMS the cluster does not itself control, and application credentials of real value should be held in an external secret manager and projected in at runtime, so that rotation, revocation and access audit live outside the cluster's own RBAC.
controls.procedure: Inventory every Secret cluster-wide with `--all-namespaces`, recording namespace, name, `type`, the key names inside `data` and the creation timestamp — reduce `data` to its key names in the same pipeline that reads it, so no secret value is ever written to the collection directory, and never place a raw dump in the deliverable. Classify by type: service-account tokens, TLS material, image pull credentials and Opaque application secrets are different risks. Record each Secret's `ownerReferences` and controller annotations, since a Secret materialised by External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver is externally sourced while an identical-looking Opaque Secret authored by hand is not. Then map consumption: enumerate containers consuming secrets through `env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef` and `envFrom[].secretRef`, since environment variables leak into crash dumps, child processes and `kubectl describe`, versus consumption through a mounted volume or the CSI driver. Establish whether an external store is in use by listing CRDs for External Secrets Operator, the Secrets Store CSI driver, Vault or Sealed Secrets, and by listing `SecretProviderClass` objects. Finally settle encryption at rest: on a self-managed control plane read the API server's `--encryption-provider-config` flag from the static pod spec and read the referenced EncryptionConfiguration on the host, checking which providers are listed for the `secrets` resource and in what order; on EKS, GKE or AKS ask the cloud provider's API instead, since neither the flag nor the file is reachable through the Kubernetes API.
api: kubectl --context <ctx> get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items |= map(.data = ((.data // {}) | keys) | del(.stringData))' > collect/secrets-meta.json

jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] as $c | ((($c.env // [])[] | select(.valueFrom.secretKeyRef != null) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, "env", .name, .valueFrom.secretKeyRef.name] | @tsv), (($c.envFrom // [])[] | select(.secretRef != null) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, $c.name, "envFrom", "-", .secretRef.name] | @tsv))' collect/pods.json

jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.volumes // [])[] | select((.secret != null) or ((.csi.driver // "") == "secrets-store.csi.k8s.io")) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, .name, (.secret.secretName // .csi.driver)] | @tsv' collect/pods.json
kubectl --context <ctx> get crd -o json | jq -r '.items[].metadata.name' | grep -Ei 'external-secrets.io|secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io|vault.hashicorp.com|sealedsecrets'
kubectl --context <ctx> -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-apiserver -o json | jq -r '.items[].spec.containers[].command[]' | grep -- '--encryption-provider-config'
controls.evidence: The Secret inventory table (namespace, name, type, key names, creation timestamp, owner references — values excluded, with the collection command shown so the reader can see values were never written to disk); the list of containers consuming secrets through environment variables versus mounted volumes or the CSI driver; the presence and provider of any external-secret CRDs and `SecretProviderClass` objects, and which Secrets are owned by them; and the encryption-at-rest evidence — either the verbatim `--encryption-provider-config` argument together with the provider list and its order for the `secrets` resource in the EncryptionConfiguration file, or the cloud API response (`cluster.encryptionConfig`, `databaseEncryption`, `securityProfile.azureKeyVaultKms`) naming the KMS key.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS requires all four, each evidenced: (a) an encryption-at-rest configuration covering the `secrets` resource whose first provider is `kms` — not `identity`, and not a local static-key `aescbc` or `secretbox` provider — read either from the EncryptionConfiguration file on a self-managed control plane or from the cloud API, where the returned KMS key identifier is non-empty; (b) no Secret whose `metadata.creationTimestamp` pre-dates the date that configuration took effect remains un-rewritten, evidenced by a later resource version or recreation timestamp; (c) every Opaque Secret is either owned by an external-secret controller — an `ownerReferences` entry or controller annotation naming External Secrets Operator, the Secrets Store CSI driver, Vault or Sealed Secrets — or appears on the client-supplied exception list; and (d) no container references a Secret through `env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef` or `envFrom[].secretRef`. Absence of retrievable encryption evidence on a managed control plane is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW, never a pass.
controls.remediation: Enable KMS-backed encryption at rest — an EncryptionConfiguration with a `kms` provider listed before `identity` for the `secrets` resource on a self-managed control plane, or the provider's envelope encryption on EKS, GKE and AKS — and then rewrite every existing Secret so it is stored re-encrypted, for example `kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -`, run from a controlled operator host rather than a shared terminal, since that command moves every plaintext value across it. Move application credentials into an external manager and project them with the Secrets Store CSI driver or External Secrets Operator, with a short synchronisation interval so rotation propagates. Switch environment-variable consumption to volume mounts. Constrain who can read Secrets under 2.11, since encryption at rest does nothing against a subject holding `get secrets`.
controls.caveat: Manual because whether a given credential should have been externalised, and what its blast radius is, is a judgement about the business that no API answers: the API can prove a Secret exists, is Opaque, and is not owned by an external controller, but only the client can say whether it holds a production database master credential that should never have been in the cluster or a value of no consequence, and only the client can approve the exception list part (c) of the verdict depends on. Three concrete traps. The base64 in `kubectl get secret -o yaml` is an encoding and nothing more, so this control is decided as much by who holds `get`/`list` on secrets (2.11) as by storage; a report that claims secrets are protected because encryption at rest is on, without stating the reader set, is misleading. On EKS, GKE and AKS the API server's `--encryption-provider-config` flag and the EncryptionConfiguration file are not reachable through the Kubernetes API at all — `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-apiserver` returns an empty list on a managed control plane, and that empty result must not be recorded as "no encryption configured" nor as compliant; go to the cloud API, and where that is out of scope the control is inconclusive rather than met. And enabling encryption only affects writes: every Secret created before the change remains in plaintext in etcd until it is rewritten, so a configuration that reads as enabled can sit over a store of plaintext secrets, which is why the verdict tests creation timestamps against the change date rather than trusting the configuration alone.

controls.title: Workload images come from approved registries and are pinned to an immutable digest
controls.objective: A mutable tag means the bytes that run tomorrow are not the bytes that were reviewed today, and an unconstrained registry means any namespace can pull an arbitrary third-party image into the cluster. Images should come from a defined set of registries, be referenced by digest so the content is fixed, and — where signing is in use — have that signature verified by an admission controller operating in enforcing mode.
controls.procedure: Extract every image reference in the cluster from three places, because they disagree: `.spec.containers[].image` and `.spec.initContainers[].image` on live pods, the same fields on every controller pod template, and the `imageID` in the pod's container status lists (`containerStatuses`, `initContainerStatuses`, `ephemeralContainerStatuses`), which carries the digest of what is actually running. Normalise each reference into registry host, repository, tag and digest, expanding an implicit host — a reference with no registry component resolves to docker.io, and one with a single path element resolves to the docker.io library namespace. Classify each against the registry allowlist supplied by the client, and flag references that use a mutable tag, the `latest` tag, or no tag at all. Record `imagePullPolicy` per container. Then determine whether any of this is enforced at admission rather than merely true today, reading the action rather than the existence of the object: Kyverno carries an action both at `spec.validationFailureAction` and, in newer releases, per rule at `spec.rules[].validate.failureAction`, so read both; Gatekeeper constraints are cluster-scoped and carry `spec.enforcementAction`, which defaults to `deny`; a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is inert until a binding names it, and that binding's `spec.validationActions` must contain `Deny` rather than only `Warn` or `Audit`; and a validating webhook enforces only where it is actually selected, so read `failurePolicy` together with `namespaceSelector`, `objectSelector` and its rules. Finally list image-pull Secrets so the report states which registries the cluster holds credentials for.
api: jq -r '.items[] as $w | (($w.spec.template.spec) // ($w.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec)) as $s | select($s != null) | ($s.containers + ($s.initContainers // []))[] | [$w.kind, $w.metadata.namespace, $w.metadata.name, .name, .image] | @tsv' collect/controllers.json

kubectl --context <ctx> get clusterpolicies.kyverno.io,policies.kyverno.io --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [(.kind // "KyvernoPolicy"), (.metadata.namespace // "cluster-scoped"), .metadata.name, (.spec.validationFailureAction // "unset"), ((.spec.rules // []) | map(.name + ":" + (.validate.failureAction // "inherit")) | join(","))] | @tsv'
kubectl --context <ctx> get constraints -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [(.kind // "Constraint"), .metadata.name, (.spec.enforcementAction // "deny (server default)")] | @tsv'
kubectl --context <ctx> get validatingadmissionpolicies.admissionregistration.k8s.io -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.name, ((.spec.validations // []) | length | tostring)] | @tsv'

kubectl --context <ctx> get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | . as $c | ($c.webhooks // [])[] | [($c.kind // "WebhookConfiguration"), $c.metadata.name, .name, (.failurePolicy // "Fail (v1 server default)"), ((.namespaceSelector // {}) | tostring), ((.objectSelector // {}) | tostring)] | @tsv'
kubectl --context <ctx> get secrets --all-namespaces --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name] | @tsv'
controls.evidence: The normalised image table — namespace, pod or controller, container, registry host after implicit-host expansion, repository, tag, digest, `imagePullPolicy` — built from `collect/pods.json` and `collect/controllers.json`; the running digest from the container status lists alongside the spec reference for each container, showing where the two differ; and the admission-enforcement evidence: Kyverno policy names with both the policy-level and per-rule failure action verbatim, Gatekeeper constraint kinds and names with `enforcementAction`, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy bindings with their `policyName` and `validationActions`, and webhook names with `failurePolicy`, `namespaceSelector` and `objectSelector`, together with the client-supplied registry allowlist the comparison was made against.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every image reference in every live pod and controller pod template resolves, after implicit-host expansion, to a registry on the client-supplied allowlist; every reference is pinned by an `@sha256:` digest; no container uses the `latest` tag or an absent tag; and at least one admission control covering all workload namespaces enforces the registry and digest requirement in a blocking mode — a Kyverno policy whose effective failure action is enforcing, a Gatekeeper constraint whose `enforcementAction` is `deny`, a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding whose `validationActions` contains `Deny`, or a validating webhook with `failurePolicy: Fail` whose selectors and rules match the workloads in question. A policy in audit, warn or dry-run mode, a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with no binding, and a webhook whose `namespaceSelector` or `objectSelector` excludes the workload namespaces all fail the enforcement condition. Where no registry allowlist has been supplied by the client, the registry half is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW rather than a pass.
controls.remediation: Replace tag references with digest references (`registry.example.com/app@sha256:<digest>`) in every manifest, and let the release pipeline compute the digest at build time so the change does not add manual work. Set `imagePullPolicy: Always` wherever a tag must remain, so the node re-resolves rather than serving a cached layer indefinitely. Add an admission policy in a blocking mode that rejects any image whose registry is not on the allowlist and any reference lacking a digest, and where images are signed, verify the signature at admission with Kyverno's image verification or a Sigstore policy controller. Mirror approved third-party images into the organisation's own registry so provenance is under the organisation's control.
controls.caveat: Manual because the allowlist is organisational policy — only the client can say which registries are approved, and a pull-through cache or mirror changes the hostname without changing provenance, so a hostname test alone cannot decide the question; the assessor must also judge whether a mirrored image's upstream is acceptable, which no API records. Five specific false passes. An image reference with no registry prefix, such as `nginx:1.25`, resolves to docker.io at pull time but contains no registry string at all, so an allowlist implemented as a hostname match finds no violation and reports every unqualified Docker Hub pull as compliant — normalise before comparing. A tag is mutable, so the spec's `image` field describes what was requested and the status `imageID` describes what is running; for a pod started weeks ago these routinely differ, and the digest is the one that matters for a vulnerability claim. An enforcement object present is not enforcement applied: a Kyverno policy with an audit failure action, a Gatekeeper constraint with `enforcementAction: dryrun` or `warn`, and a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy whose binding lists only `Warn` or `Audit` in `validationActions` are all present, healthy and blocking nothing — and a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with no binding at all does nothing whatsoever, so counting policies rather than bindings overstates coverage. A webhook that does block can still be scoped away: `failurePolicy: Fail` on a webhook whose `namespaceSelector` excludes the namespaces the workloads run in enforces nothing where it matters, and note that in `admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1` the server defaults `failurePolicy` to `Fail`, so a check that assumes an absent field means `Ignore` reports the opposite of the truth. And `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` against a mutable tag lets a node keep serving a stale, possibly vulnerable, cached layer indefinitely even after the tag has been rebuilt, so a fixed tag is not a fixed artefact.

controls.title: Every container declares CPU and memory requests and limits, and each namespace is quota-bounded
controls.objective: A container with no memory limit can consume the node's memory until the kubelet starts evicting neighbours, which is a denial of service against unrelated workloads reachable from any single compromised or merely buggy pod. Declared requests and limits give the scheduler real information and bound the blast radius; a namespace-level ResourceQuota bounds the aggregate so no single tenant can starve the cluster.
controls.procedure: Read the effective values from the live pod objects rather than from the controller templates, because a LimitRange in the namespace injects defaults at admission and the running pod may be bounded even where the template says nothing. For every container and init container cluster-wide, record `resources.requests.cpu`, `resources.requests.memory`, `resources.limits.cpu` and `resources.limits.memory`, treating an absent key as unbounded, and on clusters where pod-level resources are available also read the pod's own `spec.resources`, which can bound a pod whose per-container blocks are empty. Corroborate with `.status.qosClass`: a pod reported as `BestEffort` has no requests or limits at all anywhere in it, which is a fast cluster-wide indicator. Then list LimitRanges across all namespaces, recording `default`, `defaultRequest` and `max` per resource type, so the report can distinguish a namespace where missing limits are silently filled from one where they are simply missing; and list ResourceQuotas with their `spec.hard` keys, `spec.scopeSelector` and `status.used`, noting that a quota specifying `limits.cpu` or `limits.memory` forces every pod in that namespace to declare limits or be rejected, unless its scope narrows it to a subset of pods. Run the same test against controller pod templates so newly created pods in a namespace that later loses its LimitRange are also covered. Finally separate the pods the client cannot change — managed control-plane and cloud add-on workloads, identifiable by namespace and by owner references to a provider-managed controller — from client workloads, because the two take different verdicts.
api: jq -r '.items[] as $p | ($p.spec.containers + ($p.spec.initContainers // []))[] | select(((.resources.limits.memory // null) == null) or ((.resources.requests.cpu // null) == null)) | [$p.metadata.namespace, $p.metadata.name, .name, (((.resources.limits.memory // null) == null) | tostring), (((.resources.requests.cpu // null) == null) | tostring)] | @tsv' collect/pods.json

kubectl --context <ctx> get limitranges --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, ((.spec.limits // []) | map(.type + ":default=" + ((.default // {}) | tostring) + ",defaultRequest=" + ((.defaultRequest // {}) | tostring) + ",max=" + ((.max // {}) | tostring)) | join(";"))] | @tsv'

kubectl --context <ctx> get resourcequotas --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, (((.spec.hard // {}) | keys) | join(",")), ((.spec.scopeSelector // {}) | tostring), ((.status.used // {}) | tostring)] | @tsv'

jq -r '.items[] as $w | (($w.spec.template.spec) // ($w.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec)) as $s | select($s != null) | ($s.containers + ($s.initContainers // []))[] | select(((.resources.limits.memory // null) == null) or ((.resources.requests.cpu // null) == null)) | [$w.kind, $w.metadata.namespace, $w.metadata.name, .name] | @tsv' collect/controllers.json
controls.evidence: The per-container resource table from `collect/pods.json` giving namespace, pod, container and the four request/limit values with absent keys shown as unset, plus any pod-level `spec.resources`; the QoS class distribution from `.status.qosClass`; the per-namespace LimitRange definitions with their default, defaultRequest and max values; the per-namespace ResourceQuota `spec.hard` keys with any `scopeSelector` and `status.used`; and the separately labelled list of provider-managed pods, with their namespace and owner references, that the client cannot modify — all quoted from the collected JSON.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, across all client-modifiable pods, every container and init container in every live pod has a concrete `resources.limits.memory` and `resources.requests.cpu` value — set on the container, supplied by the namespace LimitRange `default`/`defaultRequest`, or covered by a pod-level `spec.resources` where that feature is in use; no such pod is in the `BestEffort` QoS class; every controller pod template that omits limits sits in a namespace whose LimitRange supplies them, with that dependency named in the evidence; and every workload namespace carries a ResourceQuota whose `spec.hard` includes both `limits.memory` and `limits.cpu` with no `scopeSelector` narrowing it away from that namespace's workloads. Provider-managed pods the client cannot modify are listed as an explicit exception and are neither counted as compliant nor allowed to fail the control; a run that cannot separate them from client workloads is REQUIRES_MANUAL_REVIEW for those namespaces.
controls.remediation: Set `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` for both `cpu` and `memory` on every container, sizing them from observed usage rather than guesses. Add a LimitRange to each namespace with `default` and `defaultRequest` for cpu and memory so an omission cannot produce an unbounded pod, and a `max` so no single pod can request the whole node. Add a ResourceQuota per namespace bounding `limits.cpu`, `limits.memory`, `requests.storage` and the object counts that matter (`pods`, `services.loadbalancers`). Re-roll existing workloads after adding a LimitRange, since defaults are applied at admission and do not affect pods already running.
controls.caveat: The controller template is the wrong object to read and produces errors in both directions. A LimitRange applies its `default` and `defaultRequest` at admission, so a template with no limits yields a fully bounded running pod and a template-only check reports a false finding; conversely a pod created before the LimitRange existed is still running unbounded while its template now looks compliant, which is a false pass. Read the live pod and note which namespace supplies the default. Second, a ResourceQuota that sets `limits.cpu` or `limits.memory` changes the meaning of a missing-limit finding in that namespace, because the API server then rejects any pod that omits them — but only for the pods its `scopeSelector` covers, so a quota scoped to `BestEffort` or to a priority class leaves the rest of the namespace unbounded while appearing to force limits; read the scope before relying on the quota. Third, a large share of the unbounded containers on EKS, GKE and AKS belong to provider-managed add-ons the client has no ability to patch; counting them as failures buries the client's own workloads in noise, while silently skipping their namespace hides client workloads that share it, so they must be separated by owner reference and reported as an explicit exception. Two points of precision: a memory limit set without a request causes the request to be set equal to the limit, whereas a CPU limit without a request causes throttling that presents as an unexplained latency problem, so the two resources fail differently and should be reported separately — the memory limit is the security-relevant one, since memory is the resource that evicts neighbours. On clusters where pod-level resources are enabled, a container with an empty `resources` block may still be bounded by the pod's `spec.resources`, so check that field before writing the finding. Finally, LimitRanges, ResourceQuotas and Pods are all namespaced, so every listing needs `--all-namespaces` or the assessment covers whichever namespace the selected context happens to name.
